I beg to lay upon the table the report of the minutes of the proceedings of the Imperial Conference of 1911. This ma'tter came up for discussion the day before yesterday. I called upon His Excellency the Governor General, who had just returned from a holiday, and ascertained from him that the report of the conference had naehed him that very evening. At the same time a despatch was sent to His Excellency which I have his permission to lay before the House. It is as follows:
Downing Street, 14 July, 1911.
My Lord,-I have the honour to transmit to Your Excellency, to be laid before your ministers, the accompanying copies of memorandum of conferences between the British Admiralty and representatives of the Dominions of Canada and Australia on the subject of the status of Dominion navies.
2.	This matter was mentioned at the last meeting of the Imperial Conference on the twentieth of June and it was agreed that it should he published simultaneously in this country and in Canada and the Commonwealth.
3.	I have asked the Governor General of the Commonwealth to inform me by telegraph when it is proposed to publish the memorandum there, and I shall at once telegraph to you so that arrangements may be made for a simultaneous issue of the report in Canada.
I have the honour to be, My Lord, Your Lordship's most obedient,
humble servant, (Signed) L. HARCOURT. Governor General,
* His Excellency,	.
. The Right Honourable,
Earl Grey, G.C.M.G., G.C.V.O.
A despatch anticipating this had been received a few days ago before by His Excellency to this effect:

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
subtopic: FROM MR. HARCOURT TO LORD GREY

speechtext:
London, 11th July, 1911.
Immediate.
Please inform Brodeur that it is understood by the Admiralty that time of publication of arrangement with regard to Dominion naval force would be settled in concert as was done in 1909 and that in the mean time terms will not be made public. You will be informed later as to proposed time for publication. Copy goes ito you by next mail.
(Signed) HARCOURT.
In due course this despatch was sent to the Office of External Affairs, and by *them referred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Brodeur) sent me the following letter:

Office of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries
of Canada.
Ottawa, 18th July, 1911. Sir Wilfrid T.aurier.
Prime Minister of Canada, Ottawa.
Dear Sir Wilfrid,-I beg to send you herewith copy of the despatch of which 1 spoke to you to-day, on the subject of the publication of the memorandum on the agreement arrived at between representatives of Canada and Australia on one part and the Admiralty, on the other.
I fail to sc-e why this document should not be published at the same time as the proceedings of the Imperial Conference though, indeed such may be the intention. At all events, I send you the above despatch to keep you in touch with the matter in case it should come up in the House.
Would yon be of opinion that it would be well to cable the Secretary of State asking him to hasten the publication of this document r
Yours very sincerely, (Signed) L. P. BRODEUR.
I called the attention of His Excellency to these despatches, and I stated to him that, in my opinion, I did not understand the resolution of the 20th of June, which is referred to in the despatch which I read a moment ago, as implying that the resolutions of the Defence Committee were not to be laid before the House at same time as the report of the conference. I call the attention of the House to these words of Mr. Harcourt of the 20th June, 1911:
Mr. Harcourt.-Then there is the report of the Committee of the Imperial Conference convened to discuss defence, military matters, at [DOT]the War Office. That is before the Conference now in a paper. Assuming that that report is approved, it is proposed that the precis of to-day and the proceedings of the Conference when published should contain the following statement on the matter: ' The Conference received and approved the report of the Committee on Military Defence, which had held two sittings at the War Office, under the chairmanship of the Chief of the Imperial General Staff,' and the report will he included in the papers of the Conference.
(Mr. Pearce here referred to the question of the conferences which were taking place at the Admiralty with the representatives of the Dominion of Canada and of the Commonwealth of Australia with regard to the status of the Dominions' naval forces and their cooperation with the Royal Navy, and it was agreed, on the suggestion of Mr. Harcourt, that a memorandum embodying the conclusions reached should be incorporated among the papers published in connection with the Imperial Conference.)
These resolutions of the Defence Committee were not, however, included in the report which I now lay upon the table. Having called the attention of His Excellency to this, His Excellency was pleased at once to send the following cable to Mr. Harcourt:
Your despatch of July 25, 1911, No. 573, Prime Minister will be very grateful if permission Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
could be given to lay enclosure before parliament immediately. He wishes if possible to lay it simultaneously with a full report of proceedings of Imperial Conference just received and is anxious not to have to wait till memorandum of conference on naval question is received in Australia.
Please telegraph reply as soon as possible.
(Signed) GREY.

I wish to ask the Postmaster General a question. It has been the practice for certain newspapers previous to an election to accept short date subscriptions from candidates or their supporters, and these newspapers are very generally distributed throughout the country at ordinary newspaper rates. The postal regulations state that this practice is against the regulations of the Post Office Department. Clause 62 of the regulations reads:
62 On all newspapers and periodicals posted in Canada other than those provided for in the foregoing sections, when addressed to places in Canada, the United States, or Mexico, the rate is lc. per 4 ozs. or fraction thereof to each separate address, which must be prepaid by postage stamp.
This resolution was in force previous to the last general election, but it was flagrantly violated by many of the Canadian newspapers. Clause 60 reads:
60. Copies of newspapers sent to advertisers in connection with the publication of their advertisements, and copies sent to addressss furnished by advertisers, or to persons whose subscription have been paid in whole or in part by interested parties, or marked copies, cannot be considered as addressed to sub-

scribers or as specimen copies, but are liable as transient newspapers to postage at the rate of lc. per 4 ozs. to each separate address.
I ask the Postmaster General whether it is his intention to enforce these regulations and whether he should not send out a copy of clause 60 to the newspapers of the country so that they may know if they violate that regulation they are liable to punishment.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Clause 60 shall be enforced. Any complaint that may be made to the department will be fully inquired into, and any infringement will be stopped. There is no reason why this clause should be violated by any of the newspapers. The clause shall remain as it is and it must be enforced.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: If the post office authorities are notified that the regulation is being violated, will they at once take action?

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: We all know that the law was broken immediately before the last election and that tons of mail matter were sent out by several of the daily newspapers. Of course, they knew they would receive the protection of the government, and after the election there would not be much said about it anyway. It would even up matters if the same freedom to send out this material was given to all newspapers alike immediately before the election. There might be an amended regulation, by which, for thirty days or sixty days prior to an election, this matter would be sent out at the same rate of postage as is charged on an ordinary newspaper. At all events, the regulation so long as it exists should be enforced against ail newspapers equally.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: The regulations will be enforced and I will see to it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: The answer of the Postmaster General will hardly be sufficient.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: The right hon. gentleman says ' hear, hear,' but I would remind him that the regulation was flagrantly violated by his government before the last election and the right hon. gentleman sat quietly by and said nothing about it. I was going to suggest that such a violation of this regulation at the last general election should be sufficient to warrant the Postmaster General to issue special instructions to every postmaster in this country, directing his attention to the violation which took place at the last general election, and warning him that if such a thing took place again, there would be prosecutions and dismissals.

that that be done forthwith. I may say to my hon. friend that no discrimination was made at the last general election, nor will be made if an election should take place this year. The only complain that was made to the department, if I remember well, in the last general election was against a Grit newspaper.

speechtext: I think it was published in the county of the Deputy Speaker, or in the county of my hon. friend for Grey, a local newspaper. There was a certain number of papers addressed to political friends, or to the public at large, and the complaint was made by the postmasters themselves. The postmasters are interested in seeing that a large number of papers does not come in at night and keep them at their office later than they should be. I may say to my hon. friend tha*, much to my personal regret, I had to ..nforce the regulation against that paper. There is no discrimination, there is the same law for the Grits and for the Tories.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
I would like to ask the Postmaster General a question on another point. It is a common practice-I will not charge it against one party more than another-'but I happen to know of a case where that thing was done against me, and I have no doubt possibly it may have been done in favour of the Conservative candidate in some other places. Post offices are in the habit of taking mail bags from the newspaper offices without opening them. For instance, a mail bag is sent out from Ottawa addressed to Almonte. The postal department here see the label Almonte, and takes it for granted that the newspaper office is acting honestly, and is not sending out anything but legitimate newspaper matter to regular subscribers. Unfortunately, advantage has been taken of this in many instances to put in, not merely extra newspapers addressed, or unaddressed, to persons wishing to get them in an election, but also campaign literature. I know this positively, and this literature is sent, as a rule, only to postmasters who, it is known beforehand, will accept it. 1 took the matter up on one occasion, the only time I ever made a personal charge. I personally conducted the investigation against the postmaster, and had him dismissed. His defence was that he did not hand it through the post office, that he received it in the post office mail bag and took it out and distributed it over the counter. Then I drew his attention to	the	fact that	if	he	hadplaced it	in	the hands	of	the	persons addressed through the wicket of the post office, he would have to put a half cent stamp on each one. But he thought
that because he handed it over the counter he was not obliged to put a half cent stamp on it. He had to vacate the office. I think the Postmaster General, in view of the fact that we are going into a. contest, should do his part to see that each party is treated alike.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I concur in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Sim-coe. I see no reason why, in the interest of the education of the people of this country, there should not be some special regulation on the occasion of a general election. We know that at the cost of the country there is literature going out to-day franked by the Hon. Clifford Sifton, documents that are published by a league known as the Canadian League. Now, I am not complaining of any efforts to educate the people.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: Is he violating any law?

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: No, he is not violating any law. I think perhaps he may be considered as abusing a privilege, but he bs not violating any law, and I have no complaint to make with respect to it. But if there is an election there will be one great issue, the issue will be reciprocity; and I would like to have every man, woman and child in this country who is capable at all of exercising a judgment, to have all the literature possible on both sides of the question, and then the responsibility will be upon the individual having the information. I believe it to be in the interest of the country that newspapers containing information on this subject should be circulated, and I think that the Post Office Department should make some regulation whereby newspapers can, upon the same, or proportionate terms, that they are paying the department to-day for their general circulation, be permitted to send out special issues in view of the urgency of the case, as it may exist. I heartily concur in the suggestion of the hon. member for Simcoe.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: If I may be allowed another word in reply to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Em-merson). My reason for bringing this matter up was that I know certain constituencies where wealthy candidates are running, with plenty of money, and they are able to send out, for instance, the whole of the voters' lists in their riding, and they did it at the last election to a great extent; while the candidate on the other side was not able to do anything of the kind. It was a most unfair advantage. That is one kind of literature. If hon. gentlemen could send out independent literature that was perfectly free from bias, it would be a different story.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext: I was referring to literature that could be considered as unbiased.

maintopic: QUESTIONS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman may have a different opinion to my own as to what is unbiased literature. However, that is the position I have taken. And I sincerely hope the Postmaster General will see that some instructions are issued to postmasters not to allow anything of that kind to occur.

The Hillcrest Coal and Coke Company,
Limited.
Hill Crest Mines, June 7th, 1909. Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa.
My Dear Lemieux,-On the strength of your letter of May 26th, and also of conversations with you previous to that date with reference to the strike out here I left home on June 1st and came to Hillcrest fully expecting that the mines in this district would be in operation by the time I arrived, but regret to say that things are in the same unsettled condition. I think it is outrageous that this state of affairs should be allowed to continue without the department interfering. It is true that a Board has been appointed but no agreement has been reached and it is doubtful that any will be from all that I can learn here. The mines have been idle now for over nine weeks and surely' if the Department of Labour had applied itself they could have forced matters to a conclusion before this time. I think Mr. King should appear on the ground at once and if a settlement is not reached the mine owners should be allowed to import men whom the government should protect. with soldiers. If the Labour Act is to be enforced some stringent legislation must be enacted to prevent occurrences of this kind.
I am,
Yours faithfully, (Sgd.) GEO. TAYLOR.
There is a concluding paragraph and then the signature, yours faithfully, George TayloT.'

The men are all anxious to go to work so far as I could learn, but are afraid to do so owing to the union miners preventing them. I think you should visit the ground personally and ascertain both from miners and men the true state of affairs and prepare such legislation as will for all time in future prevent the recurrence of a strike like this.
I am, yours faithfully,

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
In connection with the coronation celebration in Ottawa and the absence of the ministers therefrom I call attention to the following which appears in the Ottawa 'Journal':
Alayor's Office, June 16, 1911.-Yourself and ladies are cordially invited to enclosure on Parliament Hill on the morning of June 22, beginning at 11.15 sharp. Your presence and help upon that occasion will be very much appreciated in connection with the Coronation Day celebration.
This is the letter which the mayor dictated to his secretary in connection with the Coronation Day celebration, and which the secretary states he sent out to all the cabinet ministers who were in the city, as well as the four local members.
He ascertained the ministers who were in the city, he states, by calling up their offices. Those who were in England were not sent invitations. The others, he says, were sent invitations. .
This is the mayor's answer to the statement made by the Hon. ffm. Pugsley in the House of Commons day before yesterday, that the reason the three cabinet ministers who were in town on Coronation Day did not attend the Coronation celebration on Parliament Hill was that it was a civic affair, and they had received no invitations.
At the coronation celebration on parliament hill there were 10,000 people assembled in the presence of Lord Grey and Lady Grey, and the newspaper account of the ceremony says:
Led by Earl Grey, Governor General of Canada, ten thousand people on Parliament Hill this morning sent forth a cheer for King George V., the echo of which resounded throughout the city, and the spirit of it throughout the empire. It was Coronation Day, and in spite of the rain Ottawa citizens showred their -appreciation of the fact.
The only real lack was the absence of prominent citizens and-cabinet ministers. Earl and Lady Grey occupied a place on the flag draped platform, with a party from Government House. Mayor Hopewell was there, -and Sir Richard Scott. There was not a cabinet minister to be seen, however.
There is- Mr. Speaker a growing feeling of uneasiness1 in Canada at the anti-British attitude of this government, and that feeling has not be-en allayed by the Premier's boast in Quebec of having preserved Canada's autonomy at the Imperial Conference, and his co-olness towards pro-British proposals generally. It is a lamentable fact that

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: at the coronation ceremony in the capital of the country not a single cabinet minister thought it worth while to attend His Excellency, or to step on to the lawn in front of their offices where the celebration was being held. Indeed, it was said that some of them were looking out the windows at the ceremony in th-eir shirt-sleeves. We spent a good deal of money to send a delegation to London to participate in the ceremony there, and the people of this country will want to know why there wa-s not a cabinet minister to attend His Excellency at the Ottawa celebration. As to the statement that the ministers did not receive an invitation, whatever question there be as to that, I think they might very well have gone without an invitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
As I am one of the three ministers who enjoyed the privilege of remaining here during the two months' recess of parliament, and as this is a repetition of some newspaper attempted attacks made on some one or other, perhaps I should say a word about it. I do not know in what manner the alleged invitation to attend this function was sent to the three ministers in question, but I certainly would be a little interested to know. I have no doubt that my hon. friend the Postmaster General who was one of the three ministers who were her-e during the day of coronation would be equally glad to know whether or not the post office was utilized for the sending of the invitations. So far as I am concerned I have nothing to add to what was stated by the Minister of Public Works when this matter was mentioned in the House the other day. I do not pretend that I did not know, that there was going to be some sort of parade upon the lawn. I was at my office during each of the previous days, and I saw the building of the platform, and I should have been a very strange man if I had not supposed that it was in connection with the coronation, and that it was intended there should be some sort of celebration upon that occasion. But while that is so, and while for that reason I attach no consequence to the fact that no invitation came to me in any way in. connection with the matter, I was equally of opinion from what I saw in the newspapers that the matter was of a purely municipal or civil character. I understood an invitation had been extended to His Excellency and that His Excellency intended to be present, and that there was to be some sort of review or inspection of the Boy Scouts, and some parade of school children, and something of that sort. But that it was in any sense a government affair, or in any sense a national affair, or in any sense one that it was my duty as a minister of the Crown to attend, never occurred to

me. I am not much given to that sort of thing; I do not commonly attend such things, whether they are of a public character or something to which I would go merely as a spectator. In this instance the day being a holiday in the departments I was not in my office at as early an hour as usual, but I reached there just about when the small gathering of perhaps 150 or 200 boys and young people were separating on the lawn. If I had had the good fortune to reach the buildings a few minutes earlier, I think I should have gone to witness what was going on, but in the circumstances until somebody tried to make a great grievance of the absence of the ministers, and a slight even to His Gracious Majesty himself, it nevei occurred to me that there was the slightest importance attached to the matter one way or another. It should also be borne in mind that the fact of there being so few people present was because of a heavy rain shower in the morning, and the notifications that were put up about the city that the whole function was at an end, and that there would be no ceremony at all. I mention that, not as accounting for my own absence, because I did not know of the notices of cancellation until afterwards, but the circumstances are these I have described, and I can only say that if anybody thinks to make any political capital out of it, or to cast upon any of His Majesty's ministers in Canada aspersions as to their loyalty, it seems to me that it is about parallel to the waving of a pocket edition of the Union Jack.	[DOT]

speechtext: As I stated the other day I was informed by the Secretary of State, and by the Minister of Justice that they had not received an invitation, and the Postmaster General told me that the day after the coronation, when the whole affair was over, he did receive an invitation.

speechtext:
I cancelled an engagement I had in Montreal district to address a public meeting in order that I should be here to attend any coronation ceremonies that might take place in the capital. I received an invitation to attend the coronation dinner at Rideau Hall, and as befitting a minister of the Crown I was present with His Excellency there. Had there been an invitation received by me from the city authorities I would only have been too pleased to attend. I saw the ceremony which took place from the window of my office where I was working that day, but I may say that on my way to the office, I saw a notification posted that everything had been cancelled on account of the heavy
rain. I am surprised to see the statement of Mayor Hopewell in the newspapers that the ministers were specially notified. That is not a fact. The day after the ceremony,
I did receive at my private residence an unsigned typewritten notice stating that I would be received on the platform, if I should attend the ceremony.

speechtext: When the House adjourned ,on May 20 a supply was arranged for up to September first. I must say that since the House resumed, about two weeks ago, the business of this country has not gone along very rapidly. In the riding I have the honour to represent there are about 2,000 men employed on government public works, and I would like to know if it is the intention of the right hon. the leader of the government and the hon. leader of the opposition to make arrangements for supply before prorogation takes place. If we are to believe what we read in the daily press prorogation may take place in the very near future, and we. may have a general election at no very distant date. If anything should happen which would result in these 2,000 men being turned idle, during the early winter, I think it would be a great hardship. Therefore, I would like to know if it is 'the intention to arrange for Supply before prorogation.

WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct the attention of the hon. Postmaster General to a very important matter. Some weeks ago I put a question on the Order Paper asking how many post offices in the county of Peel were receiving less than a daily mail. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) was good enough to give an answer to the House. I am one of those who support, and will continue to support, a rural free mail delivery.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
My hon. friend the Postmaster General says hear, hear. I can show to my hon. friend that I supported a resolution in favour of a rural free mail delivery when my hon. friend voted against it in this House, but afterwards acted on the suggestion of the opposition. However, I did not rise for the purpose of discussing that. My hon. friend must remember that his department has the support of, and is contributed to, by almost every elector in Canada. The Post Office Department shows a very considerable surplus, but, in my humble opinion, that surplus is at the expense of the poorly paid postmasters in rural districts-notwithstanding the fact that since my hon. friend has been Postmaster General some increases have been made in the salaries of these rural postmasters, for which I compliment my hon. friend.
To-day we have telephones in many parts of the country, and I think my hon. friend should see to i't that a telephone is installed in every rural post office in this country where there are rural telephone systems and where the Bell Telephone Company's system reaches.
, I think in addition to an examination into the twice-a-week mail service and three-times-a-week mail service, which we have in some of the older sections, my hon. friend should see to it that we have a daily mail service to these points, and that where we have a rural telephone system there should be a telephone in each of the post offices, at the expense of the government. I think the hon. Postmaster General would receive the co-operation of the hon. members of this House, and that he would be endorsed by the people of this country if he were to introduce some system of that kind.	'

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: Is it my hon. friend's suggestion that the government should pay the rental for the telephones?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
I should say yes. I do not think it could be expected that a postmaster receiving a salary of only $35 a
Sir WILFRID LAURIER
year should be asked to contribute $10 or $15 a year for the rental of a telephone, which would be used for the general service of the community. In my opinion the rental of the telephone should be paid out of the revenue of the Dominion, in connection with the Post Office Department.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
I wish heartily to concur in the remarks made by the hon. member for Peel. Since I have had the honour of a seat in this House I have frequently called attention to the lack of proper postal facilities in my part of the country. I endorse the hon. gentleman's statement that in these older provinces, throughout the country districts wherever there are post offices, there should be a daily service, and in many places where there are no post offices they should be established. There are many reasons why the country districts in Ontario should receive more consideration than they have received in the matter of postal facilities. In many of the outlying districts the people live anywhere from five to fifteen miles trom a post office, and in many districts they get a mail only twice a week, which is practically no service at all. I think the facilities should be extended, and a daily service should be given to. all those country places. I will go further, and say that I think this government should take up the whole matter, and lay out a regular system of rural routes for post offices, and even to assist those country districts in maintaining good roads connecting many of those points. In some parts of my own constituency, the postal facilities have been so poor that the people have been obliged to put in little telephone systems of their own as their only means of communication. I have taken the trouble to compare the number of post offices in the province of Ontario in 1895 and the number in 1909, and I find that during that period the number has increased by 17 per cent. In the province of Quebec during the same period the number of post offices has Increased forty-one per cent; in Nova (Scotia, twenty-two per cent; in New Brunswick, twenty per cent; in Prince Edward Island, twenty per cent; in British Columbia, one hundred and twenty-two per cent; 'and in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, one hundred and ninety-eight per [DOT]cent. Of course, we can readily understand that in the newer sections of the country where population is rapidly increasing there would be many demands on the Postmaster General for new offices. But we find .that while the province of Onatrio has contributed more than any other province to *the revenue of the Post Office Department, the increase in the number of post offices In that province has been considerably less than in the other provinces. That strikes me as unfair. Not only is that the fact in

(regard to the province as a whole, but 1 think that very little consideration has been given to the country districts throughout that province. I am certain that so far as the county of Frontenac is concerned, they have received very little consideration. Now the Postmaster General has boasted of a surplus in the Post Office Department. I want to say that if there is one department in this country which is not entitled to a dollar of surplus it is the Post Office Department. Every dollar of the revenue of that department comes out of the pockets of the people, and I maintain that every dollar of that revenue should go back to the people in the form of increased postal facilities.
I go further, and say that if there is any department of government which would be justified in making an expenditure in excess of the revenue, that department is the Post Office Department. Therefore the boast of the Postmaster General that his department shows a surplus is a boast that, in my estimation, reflects no credit on the management of the department. I wish to raise my voice against any policy of laying up a surplus by withholding postal facilities where they are required. Now the county of Frontenac contributes considerably towards that surplus. The post offices in that county contribute nearly $4,000 a year in revenue, over and above the amount paid by the government in salaries and allowances to postmasters. I could refer the Postmaster General to some thirteen offices in the county of Frontenac where the surplus revenue over and above salaries and allowances amounts altogther to over $1,173, and the average salary paid to the postmasters in those thirteen offices is only $108 a year. None of those offices are allowed to issue postal notes or money orders, and that is a matter that I wish to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General. 1 think he is not treating the people of the rural districts fairly. I think the revenue from these post offices I refer to is large enough to warrant the Postmaster General in granting them the right to issue postal notes and money orders. I have had experience heretofore with the Post Office Department in regard to obtaining better postal facilities in my county, an experience which has not been encouraging. For instance, I asked him to establish a post office on the border of the city of Kingston at the junction of the city with the township of Kingston. I pointed out to him that within a hundred yards of the proposed location of this office there was a school, and that the daily stage went right past it. I pointed out that the cost would only be a matter of the postmaster's salary, which might be taken out of what revenue there would be from that office.
As things are now the people in the adjoining country have to travel down into
the city three-quarters of a mile to get their mail, whereas, if this office was established at, you might say, no cost at all to the government, at the point I have indicated, the convenience to the people would be very great, indeed. For a time the Postmaster General agreed to establish that office at that particular point. Apparently he was convinced that the people were entitled to that convenience. Then the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Harty) intervened and raised an objection to the post office being established just inside the city limits. He objected to the people of the adjoining country coming inside the city a matter of a few feet in order to get their mail. The point selected was the only available place for a post office. The people kept a little store and were very popular in that section. The people of Kingston in the neighbourhood of the locality signed a petition, a copy of which I have here, which was sent to the Postmaster General asking him to establish an office at that point. The people of that section of the city have their mail delivered to them two or three times a day by letter carriers. They are not asking the Postmaster General to do away with any office. The convenience to the people in the city would be very slight. It would be some convenience, I dare say, but it would be slight, whereas, the convenience to the people of the surrounding country would be very great, indeed, and the cost to the department would be practically nothing. The Postmaster General gave his consent to that, but the hon. member for Kingston objected to a post office being established within the city limits, and apparently the hon. member for Kingston was able to overcome the convictions of the Postmaster General that a post office should, in justice to the people, be established, for up to the present time, that post office has not been established.
I want to call the attention of this House to another matter. I was asked by some people living in the north of my county to bring this matter to the attention of the Postmaster General and this will serve to illustrate the lack of postal facilities in rural distri.cts. I endeavoured to have a post office established between Maberly and Sharbot Lake at a place called Fall Kiver. I asked the people to get up a petition, and I would present it. They did so, the petition was presented, and I have in my hand here now the acknowledgment from the Postmaster General of the receipt of that petition requesting the establishment of an office at that place. The letter acknowledging the petition was dated April 3, 1909. On January 18, 1910 the hon. Postmaster General sent me this letter with regard to the request for that office. I wish to place this letter upon ' Hansard ' in order that mem-

,10360
bers of this House will realize'tire difficulties in getting proper postal facilities in country districts:
Ottawa, Jan. 18, 1910.
Dear Mr. Edwards,-1 have your letter of the 13th inst., relating in part to a 'proposed post office at ' Fall River/ on lot 12, concession 7, township of Oso, county of Frontenac, at a distance of miles south from Maberly, and beg to say that it is found, on inquiry, that not more than 18 or 20 families would benefit, that it would cost $70 a year for a semi-weekly exchange of mails with Maberly, and that the office would collect a revenue of probably not more than $10. It is understood that for three or four miles the road is not open in winter between Crow lake and Fall River, and that it would, therefore, be impossible for the mail courier between Crow lake and Sharbot Lake to travel by way of the proposed office site.
In view of the cost involved, namely, $70, for the service, and $35 as the postmaster's salary, as against an anticipated revenue of only $10, the department has been unable to see its way to open an office.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) RODOLPHE LEMIEUX.
Here is a letter signed by the Postmaster General and giving as a reason for the non-establishment of this office that the department could not afford to spend possibly $90 a year in giving these people a semi-weekly service, that there are only eighteen or twenty families involved and that these eighteen or twenty families, we must infer, must remain without postal facilities, because, forsooth, the cost to the government would be $90 per year. I think I am justified in making the severest kind of criticism of the Post Office Department when they speak of the surplus of that department with such conditions prevailing in my county. I think I am justified in making the severest kind of criticism of sawdust wharf transactions, Aylesworth ditches and expenditures of money along that line when one of the members of the government will sign a letter stating that in his opinion the government would hot be warranted in expending a matter of $90 a year to give this convenience to some eighteen or twenty families. I want to read in connection with that a few words which passed between the Postmaster General and myself in this House in regard to the establishment of post offices. The hon. Postmaster General, speaking this session, as reported at pages 2143 and 2144 of 'Hansard,' said:
As regards postal facilities in a whole township, I do not know that there is any reason why the people should not be provided with these postal facilities where the distance is about five miles from a post office. It is certainly the policy of the Post Office Department to grant any request which is made with such a distance in view. Whenever my hon. friend on behalf of his own township in Frontenac or any other hon. gentleman makes a Mr. EDWARDS.
request to provide postal facilities, where there is a distance of about five miles, the Post Office Department cannot but accede to that request, and I appeal to him and to members of the House on both sides whether, whenever a request of that kind is made to the Post Office Department, it is not granted.
These are the words of the Postmaster General. In answer to his appeal I recited the case which I have recited here to-day and at the same time I expressed my pleasure at his making use of those words because I saw, or thought I saw, in those words of the Postmaster General, some hope for certain sections of my county where they have absolutely no postal facilities whatever. We had in those words the distinct promise of a minister of the Crown to relieve the situation, to grant postal facilities in places where these facilities do not at present exist.
In spite of the plain words of the Postmaster General he turns a deaf ear regardless of his own statement. I would not be doing my duty to my constituents if I did not under the circumtances state the facts in this House. I do not think that the people in the country districts have received proper and just treatment from the Post Office Department. I want to be most emphatic in being understood that I do not think the Post Office Department is entitled to boast of any surplus. The money comes from the people, and the money should go back to the people in increased postal facilities. I want to- impress also on the Postmaster General and the members of the House the further fact, that the relative increase in the population of the various provinces does not in my estimation warrant the great difference which prevails in the increase of the number of post offices granted to the various provinces-. If we consider the increase of the population of Ontario and of the other provinces, between 1895 and 1909, and if we take into consideration, as we have a -right to, the post office revenue obtained from these various provinces, then, I say it is worthy at least of a little thought on our part, that the increase in the number of the post offices in the province of Ontario-which contributes most towards the revenue of the post office, which has the largest population and the greatest wealth -is relatively much less than the increase in the number of post offices in any of the other provinces. Taking the years 1905 to 1909, there has been an increase of 17 per cent in the number of post offices in the province of Ontario, an increase of 41 per cent in the province of Quebec, an increase of 22 per cent in Nova Scotia, an increase of 20 per cent in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, an increase of 122 per cent in British Columbia, and an increase of 198 per cent in -Manitoba and the prairie provinces. I

appeal again to the Postmaster General to give the country districts more consideration in the matter of increased postal facilities, than he has given in the past. I -would rather not have to adversely criticise, but I do not think I would be doing mj duty, if I allowed this opportunity to pass without saying a word on behalf of the people'of my county. I am perfectly sincere, in making this statement that whatever has been done in the way of improvement-and a good deal has been done in various parts of the country-I do not think that more consideration has been given to the cities and towns than has been given to the country districts. This or any other government would be well advised in establishing well defined postal routes in the country districts, and I think a considerable sum of money might well be expended bv this government in helping to maintain the roads on these well established postal routes. A post office means a great deal to the people of a rural district. I have no objection whatever to the free rural mail delivery routes, and I think it is a step in the right direction, but I do saj that before free rural mail delivery is given to these centres which now have a daily service, or even more than a daily service, consideration should be given to these sections of the country where the people get their mail only twice or three times a week. I believe in giving to the various districts a daily mail and then extending your free rural mail delivery limits just as rapidly as your finances will permit. If the Postmaster -General or any member of this House, tells me that greater postal facilities cannot be given to any section of my county, because so much money has to be expended on free rural mail delivery routes, that they cannot afford to give proper facilities to the outlying districts, then I think it is my duty to state here my objection to such a policy. I hope the Postmaster General will give this matter the consideration it deserves.

My intention is to continue that until it is raised to $50. I am heartily in favour of the extension of the rural telephone system, because 1 know the advantages which would accrue from it. In the county of Nicolet, which I once represented in this House, I found
in nearly every parish a good system of rural phones, and it was a great facility to the people. In many European countries, and even in Japan, the Postmaster General is called the Minister of Communications, and has under his control not only the mail system, but the cables, telegraphs and telephones. In these countries the system works well and it pays well although the rates are far from being high. The day may not be far distant when in Canada a similar system will prevail. Speaking for myself only, I am personally in favour of a government controlled rural telephone system. I think it would be quite an addition to the advantages now enjoyed by the farmers. I think public opinion in the country, especially in the western provinces and in Ontario, is shaping itself in that direction. For my part I have no hesitation in stating that I would view with favour the establishment of a rural telephone system, under the control of the Post Office Department. Of course this is only my personal opinion, and I do not wish to commit any one but myself to it.
As regards the service in the older sections of the province, I would like to answer the mild arraignment of my hon. friend. I think I am right in saying that whenever it has been shown to me that an extension of the service should be made, I have never hesitated in granting the request. As a matter of fact I can state that for the last year at least, it has been an excsptional case when I refused such a request. I consider that a semiweekly or tri-weekly service in the older sections of the country at the present time is an out of date system, -and should be replaced by a jnore modern one. My hon. friend (Mr. Edwards), spoke a moment ago in reference to the average number of post offices opened in the new provinces as compared with the older provinces. I must shy there is some truth in the statement of the hon. gentleman, but, the explanation is not very clear. The postal system has been in vogue in the older sections of the community-in the eastern part of Canada as we call it-for over a century; since the time of Benjamin Franklin, who was the first Postmaster General. In the new provinces those people who come from the, old country ask to have the postal facilities as they had them in England. This is not a matter to he trifled with. We must meet their legitimate demands. We bring them to the western provinces by advertising our country, and having brought them there the least we can give them is proper postal facilities. I may tell the House that up to the present time I have not refused one per cent,of the requests which have been made for new offices in the western districts. I might

say that same thing for New Ontario and New Quebec.
My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), compared the number of post offices in Ontario and Quebec. I hope my hon. friend does not think I am in any way sectional in connection with this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I must confess that I am not a little surprised at the communication that has been read to the House by the hon. member. It seems to me that it was written without a full knowledge of the Act. In reading over the letter carefully, I find that it has reference only to one part of the Act. The letter states:
There is no provision in the act authorizing any court to declare what the forfeiture shall he, and I can find no provision covering the matter in any statute, and it seems to me that the offence being a statutory one, there must be jurisdiction conferred upon a court or courts authorizing a declaration of what the forfeiture shall be. That is exactly what is in the Act at present. The Act contains two methods whereby it may be enforced. The first is:
The sum forfeited may, with the written consent of any judge of the court in which the action is intended to be brought, be sued for and recovered as a debt by any person who first brings his action therefor in any court of competent jurisdiction in which debts of like amount are now recovered.

the penalty, and suggests an alternative. The very next section has in it exhctly what he is suggesting. The first method is the recovery of the penalty as a debt, the second is the recovery on summary conviction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very much interested in this question. As the hon. minister knows1, I brought to the attention of this House on

two or three occasions instances in which there had been wholesale infractions of the law. I have also- pointed out the manifest injustice and futility of an Act the administration and enforcement of which is left to private individuals, who in the majority of cases do not care to take the trouble or the financial risk involved in working up a case against a large corporation, not to speak of the risk of an adverse verdict. As far back as July, 1908, a former Minister of Labour, the present Postmaster General, realizing the cogency of the position I then took, promised that the situation would be reviewed, by the department, and that legislation would be introduced as speedily as possible to remedy the defects in the law which I then pointed out. Nothing further has been done, and the same conditions continue to obtain throughout the length and breadth of Canada. We had an instance of that only a few months ago which I brought to the attention of my hon. friend, and I think he promised an investigation into it. It was a case in which men were brought by the score almost from across the boundary at Sault Ste. Marie to displace Canadian workmen who had been there for many years, and against whose work alone no objection could be found. Those men were aliens, brought to Canada in defiance of the law, but no one cared to take the risk involved in fighting the gigantic corporation which had brought them in, and, therefore, the matter was not brought to the attention of the department. These importations could be easily prevented. Just as the Department of Immigration places officers on the frontier to watch for undesirable immigrants, why could not the Department of Labour place inspectors at different points along the frontier to make reports on these matters, and, thereby minimize if not entirely prevent the infractions of this law? If the Alien Labour Law is a serious law and the Minister of Labour is serious in his attempts to enforce it, why does he not enforce it? If he finds that private individuals do not take enough interest in the law to enforce it-and I do not blame them- why does he not himself take power, if he considers he has not sufficient already, to attend to the enforcement of his own law? The members of this government are usually not lacking in vigilance in matters of this kind except where provincial authority is concerned. We have a very cogent instance of that in the administration of the Election Law. When my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) commented on the government's inability to enforce laws which it placed on the statute-book, the answer was: The laws are there, and they should be enforced by the provinces; that is what the judicial machinery of the provinces is for. How does that apply to the-enforcement of the Dominion Elections Act? The Minister of Justice told us in this House that he was perfectly justified two or three years ago in sending at the expense of this government on election day policemen on a special train in order, as he said, to prevent any violation of the Election Law at the polls. If it is competent for this government to do that in one case, why can it not do it in another case which is of manifest interest to' the whole of Canada? I sincerely hope that this serious niatter will be dealt with in the manner in which it should be. The minister's contention is that the remedy is entirely in the hands- of the workingmen. Take the one instance of the man who had the hardihood to prosecute a large lumber corporation at Blind River for the infraction, of the Act. He had to go to the expense of going to Blind River, subpoenaing witnesses and employing counsel, and when he was able to get a conviction, and the corporation was fined $50 of which $25 went to the prosecutor, all of this $25 was exhausted in the expense of prosecuting. What encouragement is that to a man getting $2 or $2.50 a day to take upon himself the whole burden of the enforcement of that law? What the department says is: Go ahead, take all the risks, employ counsel, go on with the evidence, and if you succeed we will give you one-half of the penalty that may be imposed, entirely losing sight of the fact that these men are labouring men who are absolutely unable to lose the time, and the money involved in a prosecution; and if there be not a conviction, who is to pay the man the expenses- involved? This is a view of the matter upon which I have not yet heard the Minister of Labour comment-the risk imposed upon a class of men who are. least able to bear it; and if the minister is sincere and honest in his desire to relieve the workingmen, to prevent injustice being done, and to secure the enforcement of a workable Act, which will be for the benefit of Canada generally, and the working classes in- particular, he will adopt some method, as was promised three years ago, by which this Act will become more workable and more enforceable.

Mr. Speaker, in connection with this matter, I would like to draw the attention of the minister to- two prosecutions which were instituted by private parties in 1905 against the Cape Breton Electric Company. The hon. minister will doubtless appreciate the difficulty that must exist where individuals 'are called upon to enforce their rights under an Act as cumbersome as that now under discussion. Leave must be obtained from a county court judge before proceed-

ings can be begun either before a magistrate or before the judge himself. That means an application to the judge in any event, and before that can be made, counsel must be employed, the order must be served on the company, and then the procedure must go on from that to the trial. This involves loss of time, and a great deal of expense, varying from $75 to $200 or $300, depending on the number of -witnesses and the distances they have to travel. That is not all. The individual who brings an action against his employer need never again seek employment from that employer or even from any other in the locality. He becomes black-listed. It is only in districts where complete organizations exist for the defence of labour that prosecutions can be brought under the Act at all.	It is unfair
to keep on the statute-book any longer an Act so expensive to - the individual that in view of the fact that it has been in operation so many years, the minister, going back ten years, can only cite the number of cases he cited this afternoon as having been carried to a successful conclusion.

Well, the fact of the matter is that, as this is an Act for the protection of the labourer, the protection of those who belong to the country, and who belong to the flag, it should be the duty of some person to enforce it. Collectors of customs guard the ports of entry, and we have a fishery protection service. It is not left to the fisherman to lay a charge against those who encroach on the country's fisheries. There seems to be some one appointed to administer every one of the country's laws except this Alien Labour Law. 'In the United States when a person lands from a boat or a train, he is almost always interrogated, especially if he has the appearance of being an artisan or labourer and he is asked as to his object in entering the country; and again and again many of them have been turned back. In this country no such safeguards are organized to protect the labourer, and the individual labourer in a country village or small manufacturing town where there are no organizations, is left the burden. It is left to him as an individual to prosecute parties, perhaps, a powerful corr>r>ration; who will take appeal after appeal, and he is a wise labourer who will look at the Act, and forget its existence, and bear the burden. It would be folly for the ordinary workingman to assume the responsibility of prosecution under such an Act as that, and hope to come out successfully. I do not urge this matter in a party spirit, but I think Mr. MADDIN.
I am making a wholesale criticism of the administration. I hope the minister will take it seriously to heart, and if he ever gets another opportunity before this parliament, which is very doubtful, he will see to it that the Act is amended and improved.

One result of the agreement already has been the enhancement of the value of fruit lands in the Okanagan.
Mr. Martin Burrell, a member of the House and a fruit grower, owned a 160-aere farm, with a partially-bearing orchard, and offered it for sale about a year ago for $20,000. I am quoting now from the Victoria 'Times,' the organ, I believe, of the hon. friend. He added:
Another instance which I am able to vouch for also, is that of the Matt Miller ranch, sold for $200 an acre on May 5 last, although a man had been given the refusal of it at $100 an acre several months before, showing that some people are not afraid of any evil effects to the fruit industry because the duty is to be taken off fruit. (Applause.)
I will just deal with the last paragraph first. The minister says: that he is able to vouch for this statement. This Tanch is in Kettle River valley where I live. I know the circumstances absolutely and I am, in my place in this House, prepared to say, and to make affidavit, if necessary, that his statement that the ranch was sold for $200 an acre after reciprocity was announced and that it had been offered for $100 before, is absolutely untrue, and that the second price was simply the first price, namely, $100 an acre. I may further add that the man who made the second proposition after . reciprocity was announced fell down in his deal. These are the absolute facts that the minister can find out for himself. Yet he goes on to say that he can vouch for a statement of that kind. Let me deal with the statement he made about my own affairs and I do it for the reason, that I find that up and down the country in the Liberal press, this statement of the minister has been reported without the denial which was given to it by myself. It was given prominenqe in paper after paper after he had held this meeting. 1 think it a most disgraceful thing that a minister should make an unsupported statement on false Pretenses dragging in my private affairs, and then that no correction shall be given to it in the Liberal press published in Winnipeg and elsewhere. Mr. BURRELL

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
I had no intention to interfere with the private affairs of my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) when I used as an argument the statement that he had sold his fruit ranch at an enhanced price, nor do 1 think that any one could construe my using this alleged fact into an interference with his private business. The report that Mr. Burrell had sold his fruit ranch at Grand Forks at a very good price to a company that were going to engage in the fruit business appeared in the British Columbia newspapers, and I wrote to ascertain the facts from a responsible gentle* man in Grand Forks, and the statement I made at Nelson and Fernie that Mr. Burrell had held his ranch at a certain figure previous to the announcement of the reciprocity pact, and that he had sold it several months after the announcement of reciprocity at an advance of $10,000, was given to the public on the authority of a letter which I have still in my possession from a very prominent resident of Grand Forks who inquired into the facts. I will
accept the word of the hon. member that he has not sold his fruit ranch at an enhanced price. It is none of the business of the public at what price he sold his ranch, but if it is a fact that he did sell it at an enhanced price after the announcement of reciprocity, as the general opinion is in the neighbourhood of Grand Forks, dt would be fair and legitimate to mention it as an argument in favour of the benefit of reciprocity to the fruit business. The hon. gentleman h ad an excellent ranch and the statement is that he sold it at a very good price, and that those who bought it are going into the growing of fruit on a still larger scale than he. It is a fact that the other ranch to which I referred was negotiated for at an. enhanced price, and that in the neighbourhood of Nelson a small ranch has been sold at $750 an acre, although that may be accounted for in part by the fact that it is beautifully situated on the lake and very desirable for a residence. The fact remains that the removal of duty on fruit, has not tended to depreciate the value of fruit lands in British Columbia, but on the contrary has caused the prices to go higher. The price of fruit lands immediately south of the boundary line is I believe from 50 per cent to 100 per cent higher than the price of fruit lands in relatively as good a position north of the boundary line. I 'used these statements on the public platform. I admit the information is second-hand, but the hon. gentleman himself knows better than I do about it, and I would suggest that he might take the public into his confidence, and tell the people the circumstances, not contenting himself with making a general denial. I do not think there is any divulging of private business about it. There is not a land transaction in British Columbia that the price is not published in the newspapers. Probably the hon. gentleman (Mr. Burrell) regrets that he has sold his fruit 'lands so soon. The price of fruit land, in the Boundary Creek country and _ the Okanagan Valley, is higher to-day than it was 5 months ago, and I am quite positive that there has been no depreciation in the price of these lands in consequence of the reciprocitv agreement. I have no desire to interfere 'with my hon. friend's private affairs nor did I think I did so when I made use of the argument. Now, in reference to the other matter, the hon. gentleman has said that the Yale-Cariboo election might be held on the same day as the other elections throughout the Dominion, and I am inclined to agree with him. The difficulty in Comox-Atlin is that the ballots cannot be sent around that district in the week intervening between nomination day and polling day. It certainly could not be done at my by-election which was held in the winter. I question if it could be done in

an interval of two weeks. There are places up the Skeena Kiver where the people have to travel by dog train in winter and it takes two or three weeks for them to get their mail, but of course in summer it is more easily accomplished, and, if it can be done, and if nomination and polling can be fixed on the same day as the other elections, I am absolutely, in favour of it, because I do not think there is anything to be gained by deferring an election. It must be remembered that Oomox-Atlin is i,000 miles long by the route travelled from Alberni on {lie Southwest corner to Atlin on the Northeast, and it comprises 150,000 square miles in which there are 100 polling places, and in the case of Queen Charlotte Island a steamer has_ to go around delivering the ballots. If it is at all possible, I am of opinion that the election should be held on the same day as the other elections.

Mr.	TAYLOR	(New	Westminster).	I	.
cannot say with certainty as to what is held up to the Minister of Inland Revenue as I have no knowledge of his inner conscience, and private acts, but I can say from my own knowledge that Mr. Kelly is held up, if not to the minister, to all the rest of the community as the chief beneficiary of what in vulgar parlance is called the graft upon the government at Vancouver. That is a matter of public knowledge, discussed by Robert Kelly himself in his evidence, and accepted by him as being common property. It seems incredible that when all the rest of the world knows it, and when Mr. Kelly admits it, that the minister from British Columbia after all his intimate relations with Mr. Kelly should never have heard it. Here we have an interpreter .suspended to make possible the discovery of the frauds; suspended on evidence so substantial that the very thing predicted turned out, and on this ship from which he was excluded they discovered over twenty bogus merchants, each of them having a letter to Yip On, the suspended interpreter, and a bag of gold to be given to him. All these were exposed as frauds by the suspension of this interpreter, and yet the minister from British Columbia, who should have been the first to. put a stop to these frauds, which according to public rumour had been going on then for three years, and perhaps longer, allowed Bob Kelly to send this telegram:
Most important that Yip On shall be continued as Chinese interpreter.
Most important to whom? Not to the public, because the public were making $500 a head, out of these twenty men coming in at that moment, and which they would not have made had it not been for the suspension of Yip On.

speechtext:
In. regard to the dispute between the hon. minister and myself, I think I have proved the case absolutely. On the 20th of September we have an official report from Foster to Sherwood, his chief, that the discovery was made of Yip On's rascality at Victoria. That was no matter of secrecy. It was on the tongue of every employee in the customs service, and they were making a regular hubbub in Vancouver. Is it conceivable that these gentlemen, the heads of the patronage committee in Vancouver, should be closeted with the hon. minister on such serious business, on the night of the 20th September, and have no knowledge of a matter officially communicated from Vancouver that very day by Foster to his chief, Sherwood? I say the evidence is indisputable that these gentlemen knew all about the discovery of Yip On's complicity in this transaction befote the date of this telegram. It is impossible that it should be otherwise. Of course, I cannot say that the hon. minister knew, but I go back to my former premises that it is an act of the most gross impropriety, in a matter so grave as this, for him to allow his name to be used, and telegrams to be sent in his name by any person whatever, least of all by persons bearing the character of these men with respect to these matters in Vancouver.
Apparently the patronage committee at Vancouver got very busy, as will appear from the following:
Sept. 23, 1910.

friends unanimous for Yip On. Think dept, acting unwisely.
