speechtext: Is any reason given as to why Yip On should be put back into the service?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: No reason whatever is stated as to why he should be put back. There was a reason stated why Lew should not be continued as interpreter, and that was because all these gentlemen represent him to Ottawa as being a person of bad character. In the light of the revelations respecting Yip On, it seems to me their judgment is somewhat defective. In any event the fact remains that it was most important that Yip On should be reinstated in the public service, notwithstanding the fact that he had been caught red-handed in this rascality at Victoria. It is a peculiar thing that we have the hon. minister from British Columbia (Mr. Templeman) lending himself to the suggestion.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: When was the first information that documents incriminating Yip On were in the possession of the government, before or after this?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
Before this. The explosion at Victoria took place on the 18th September, when the new interpreter and inspector went on the ship and discovered these incriminating documents. On his return to Vancouver two days after the discovery he made his official report. This is where our friend Bob
Kelly comes in. He engaged in the attempt to paralyse the inspector by giving him as an associate the man primarily responsible for the frauds, and who, of course, would prevent him from making any further discovery.
We had an argument in this House the other day as to whether or not the minister sent a telegram asking for the discontinuance of the investigation. The argument was invited by himself, because when In arose, it seems to me with a guilty conscience, he put these words in my mouth, when as a matter of fact I had not said anything of the kind. What I had said was that the minister sent a deterrent telegram to the department at Ottawa. He immediately rose to say it was absolutely untrue that he had sent any telegram asking for the stopping of the investigation. I ask any reasonable man whether that is not playing upon words, whether it can be dignified by any better term than quibbling, when a minister and his associates sent telegrams which in effect would stop any effective investigation although in express terms they did not say so, to make the bald denial in the Blouse that they ever sent any telegram advising the stopping of the investigation. This would have been the wrong term to use in any event because according to the minister himself, Inspector Foster had completed his investigation; having obtained sufficient evidence to justify the further inquiry, which, at Mr. Foster's request, was held by this Royal Commission. Yet we find the minister asking to have Yip On reinstated to continue for seven years more the irregularities which ne and his associates had carried on for seven years unchecked. With further reference to whether or not this had the effect of stopping the investigation I would like to read to the minister the evidence of one of his friends.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
The hon. member has denied that he had suggested that 1 had used any influence to stop the investigation. The hon. gentleman said:
This shows how carefully the ministers of the Crown, under this government, administer their departments, when a minister will deliberately advise his colleagues to stop investigation into a fraud of this kind.
That is what I denied.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: I think the minister did advise, in effect, the stopping of the investigation. I will read from his friend, Harry Senkler, to show that he, too, thought he advised his colleagues to stop the investigation and I could read other evidence to show that that belief was wide spread.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: Read it all.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: The evidence here would take 200 hours to read.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: Then do not, make insinuations.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
I am not making insinuations; I am making direct statements. Mr. Senkler, at page 366 of the evidence, question 2895, said:
Q. Do you, of your own knowledge, or through your association with members of the Liberal party in this city, know or believe that there are any men profiting; by graft through Chinese immigration frauds?- A. I do not believe there is any as far as the Liberal Association or its members are concerned. From what appears in the papers it may be there is money beihg made out of this Chinese business, but if so it has been done by people who had no connection with the Liberal Association, either personally or any other way.
Q. And it has been done in such a way that the Liberal Association has known aiotliing about it?-A. Then when this matter first came up the matter of the investigation there, when, I think you, Mr. Grant, and Mr. Farris acted as counsel, I was away and while I was away there was one telegram sent in my name by some individual members of the committee to Ottawa which was, I think, that this investigation should not go on.
There was the interpretation of a telegram identical in terms with that of the minister, translated by the man in whose name it was sent ' which was, I think, that this investigation should not go on.' Now, I ask the House whether I am justified in forming the imprsssion formed by the very gentleman in whose name the deterrent telegram was sent.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext: What was the reason suggested why the investigation should not go on?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
There was no reason suggested, simply an urgent request that Yip On should be reinstated as interpreter.
If there is one member of this House, and I am glad there is one, who comes out of this business creditably, so far as his personal actions are concerned, that member is the first minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). He turned a deaf ear to all the remonstrances of all his influential friends on the coast. I shall read some correspondence with him.
(Private.)
Prime Minister's Office, Ottawa,
October, 3, 1910.
My Dear Senkler,-I write you with reference to the Chinese frauds, as to which you have telegraphed me. On receipt of your telegram I communicated at once with the Department of Trade and Commerce and there found that there was a very strong prima facie case against the Chinese interpreter, and that he had been properly suspended. I Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
cannot, therefore, understand why these frauds should not be exposed. The public are so keen about this Oriental business that we will put ourselves in very serious trouble if we were to create the impression that we are not doing our full duty to have the law faithfully carried out. If you have any reason to think otherwise,, please write to me and give me your full views.
Let me avail myself of this opportunity to again offer you my sincere thanks for the great assistance which you gave me and my friends in our last visit to British Columbia.
Believe me, ever,
My dear Senkler,
Yours very sincerely, WILFRID LAURIER,
J. H. Senkler, Esq., K. C.,
Vancouver, B.C.
While the minister from British Columbia, on the ground /at Vancouver, had made most diligent inquiry as he said, and had found no reason why Yip On should not be reinstated, and took the trouble to authorize -that telegram, the first minister, 3,000 miles away, had found that there was a very strong prima facie case against the Chinese interpreter, and that he had been properly suspended.
The following is from Mr. Senkler:
(Personal.)
October 8, 1910.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier,
Ottawa, Ontario.
My Dear Sir Wilfrid,-I have your telegram of the 26th of September, which reads as follows:
' Sorry cannot agree with you. Have looked into matter and prima facie case against Yip On so strong as to warrant suspension, matter will be looked into again but meantime suspension must be maintained.'
That was Sir Wilfrid's attitude from the beginning:
I presume that this was in answer to a telegram which was sent to you in my name by the executive of the association on the 23rd of the same month. It also seems that a further telegram was sent by the committee in my name on the 24th of September, but whether it was sent to yourself or to Sir Richard Cartwright, I have not been able to find out. As a matter of fact, I think the committee were wrong in sending a telegram of that kind in my name in my absence. It they thought so strongly on the matter as they apparently did, they should have sent it in the name of the secretary, or vice-president, or acting chairman. However that may be, I desire to write you in connection with mv ideas thereon.
I personally do not know very much about the former interpreter for the government, Yip On. He has been a witness in one or two matters that I have been connected with, but otherwise I know nothing about him. Chinese interpreters, as well as most others of the same nationality are, in my opinion, proverbially dishonest and need a great deal of watching, and if it were at all possible to obtain a Chinese interpreter who is not a Chinaman, it would be infinitely preferable to one of the Chinese race.

(Paragraph left out.)
I wish also to draw your attention to the fact that a message came to the press of this city from Ottawa, that the Liberal committee of this city Mr. Ralph Smith and Mr. Templeman were all endeavouring to stop the investigation which was started in connection with the immigration of Chinese. I, of course, cannot tell you how this dispatch ever came to be sent, but it is entirely^wrong so far as our committee, at any rate, is concerned. When I returned home and found what had been done I called a further meeting of the committee, and every man of the committee agreed that a thorough investigation into this matter should be taken, and, when I was approached personally by the press in connection with it, I told them so, and had the dispatch from Ottawa flatly contradicted.
I am to-day writing you in answer to your letter of the 12th of September.
Yours very truly.
This is not signed, but it is evidently the duplicate copy of Mr. Senkler's letter. In passing I may mention that this is one of the gentlemen said to have been in the room in the Vancouver Club when the Templeman telegram was sent.
Now we will return to the commissioner. He gives a long inner history of the proceedings taken to ensure exnosur" ' these frauds. On page 30 of his report he says:
Concurrently with these wires, however

That is, the wires to Ottawa announcing
the discoveries



events [DOT] were happening at the coast
which gave Messrs. Mclnnes and Lew considerable trouble and out of which grew the charges against the lion. Mr. Templeman, and the members of the Liberal executive hereinbefore outlined. Some inkling of Mr. Mclnnes' activities leaked out in Vancouver, and Mr. R. Kelly heard of them. His information was that Mr. Mc-Innes was endeavouring to oust Yip On for the purpose of installing D. Lew in his place, and that the charge was desired not from any desire to improve the service, but for the personal benefit of those seeking to brim' it about. (See Kelly, p. 3108, q. 34275-6, and p. 3133, q. 34427-32.) To test Mr. Kelly's candour on this matter, Mr. Grant was specifically requested by the commission to cross-examine in reference thereto. (See Kelly, p. 3144, q.
34504)	. The result is set out at pp. 3145, q.
34505)	, and shows, that Mr. Kelly believed what he alleged.
It was well known in Vancouver that there was great rivalry between the Canadian Pa-cifio railway steamship line and the Blue Funnel line to secure the Chinese passenger traffic. It was known also that Yip On's uncle was the Canadian Pacific railway agent for Chinese passenger traffic in Vancouver, and that Sam Kee, a friend of Mr. Lpw, acted in a similar capacity for the Blue Funnel line. As will be seen later, the interpreter could do a great deal in the way of influencing the passenger traffic to one'of the other line by making entrance of incoming Chinese difficult or easy at his pleasure. Mr. Kelly from the information lie had of the 328i
activities of Mr. Lew, believed his object was to secure control of the post of interpreter for the "benefit of the Blue Funnel line (see Kelly, 3134, q. 34429-31), and (p. 3145, q. 34,507-9, and p. 3146, q. 34509-10) and from other information he had, he believed Mr. Mclnnes was the man behind the whole investigation from the start, and that Mr. Mclnnes had brought it about and was active in it, not for any improvement in the public service, but to further his personal interests (p. 3110, q. 34276, and p. 3145, q. 34508).
These two beliefs actuated Mr. Kelly in what he did. The motive he attributed to Mr. Lew was not proven before the commission, but sufficient was proven to indicate that Mr. Lew had his eye on the position of interpreter.
Good Mr. Kelly-Mr. Kelly, the saviour of his country, the leader of Tammany, so reformed that he would foil this great evil, would nersuade the minister to send telegrams in his name, and would send wild expostulations in his own name, because he thought some person had some personal end to serve by his recommendations to the government! Is there anybody in Vancouver except this commissioner who would write in that way of Mr. Kelly? Can we attribute this to anything except the inherent good nature of one Irishman, Denny Murphy, dealing with another Irishman. Bob Kelly? I do not think this has been taken anywhere for anything but a joke. I think again the commissioner has been overwhelmed by the political asssociations connected with his appointment. Here is what he says of another hero:
Just at this juncture Mr. Templeman came to Vancouver, and at a dinner at the Vancouver Club, on the evening of either September 20th or September 21st, probably September 20th, 1910, met Messrs. Kelly, Senkler, McDonald and others. After dinner he went in'o a room with the three named. He was informed by them that Yip On had been suspended, and that Mr. Lew, who he was told was crooked, was acting in his place, and was whollv unfit for such a position of trust, because of his undesirable character. Further that the investigation was practically over, and that nothing in particular had been elicited against Yip On. (Templeman. p. 3436 and 3437). As to this last statement, whilst as will be seen, Mr. Foster had failed to get any legal evidence against Yip On, he did have in his hands moral proof, if credited, of his complicity in the frauds. The parties interviewing the minister had not approached Mr. Foster to ascertain what he had because of their belief, justified in the opinion of the commission, that he was being used to promote the Mclnnes' intrigue. (Kelly a. 3144, q. 34502-06). Instead they had inter-[DOT]iewed Mr. Bowell, comptroller, and Colonel Worsnop, surveyor of the port of Vancouver, and Dr. Munro, medical inspector, who all assured them of their thorough belief in Yip On's honesty. (Kelly, p. 3130, q. 31394-7). The fact, however, that Mr. Foster had not been seen must have been told to the minister by his interviewers, for some of them as will

be seen, went with him very shortly after the interview, when he set out to ascertain what Mr. Poster really had discovered. (Glover, p. 2479 at top, and Templeman, p. 3448, q. 36,557,-60.
I would like to contrast that with the minister's statement a little while ago that I had misplaced the date-that at that time nothing had been discovered; that ne had sent his telegram first and the discovery had come afterwards. I have proved conclusively by the evidence that the minister was wrong, and I have now the same statement by Commissioner Murphy himself, that Mr. Templeman, after hearing these revelations in the private room at the club, said he had set out to ascertain what really Mr. Foster had discovered-a wise precaution, but which had no effect from the fact that before he set out to see what had leaked out he sent the message to his colleagues instructing them what must be done, what was most impoitant in the interest of some person not yet disclosed.
Whilst there is no direct evidence that Hon. Mr Templeman was told of the suspicions entertained against Mr. Mclnnes, it would seem that he was, from Mr. Kelly's evidence (page 3113, q. 34287) and from the minister's statement that the fear expressed to him as a reason for asking prompt action on his part was that Mr. Lew's permanent appointment to the interpretership was then imminent at Ottawa (Mr. Templeman, page 3437, q. 36533). Because of this fear, Hon. Mr. Templeman sent a wire (ex. 417) to Sir Richard Cartwright recommending the reinstatement of Yip On (Mr. Templeman, page 3438 at top page).
I was going to refer to some of the criti-ism of Mr. Foster by the commissioner, but first must read a letter from the police inspector, found on page 34 of the evidence. Mr. Foster's letter throws so much light on the inner history of the investigation that, in so far as it refers to Chinese matters, it is here set out verbatim.
Ottawa, November 10, 1910.
Dear Friend Lew,-Your letter of November 2 received to-day. I showed it to Sherwood and he had a copy made and he took it to O'Hara. I was just speaking to O'Hara for a few minutes. He was greatly pleased with our work, he told me there was going to be a Royal Commission appointed sure. I had a talk with T. McL, he states you are not the only target that they are firing at from Vancouver, for he has had to stand some pretty hot shots; he says he had the necessary papers to prove them liars, they had him before the Premier twice. Sherwood said when I was talking to him the day I got home that O'Hara wanted to have a talk with me, and he would let me know when he would see me, but so far I have heard nothing about him meeting me. They seem to be leaving everything to the commission. I was talking to Tom again to-day, and he stated that he had a talk with O'H. yesterday, but Tom is Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
afraid Templeman will stop the Royal Commission when he returns from the west, if he can, but X think Temp, say is pretty small or in other words he is a lightweight in this case and particularly with O'Hara now since he has the record of your successor, who is Temple-man's appointment. I am returning card, Sher. wood said it was not necessary to have a writing expert compare the writing for O'Hara, and he also was convinced what you stated was correct. Sherwood also stated Canadian Pacific railway were going to look fully into your case,. You seem to have Sherwood and O Hara on your side now, hut you know you are still in the hands of the politicians.
I was summoned from Edmonton to Chicago the first of November as fingerprint expert to give evidence at a murder trial. I was able to swear positively to the prints, I was there for two days, but I left as soon as I got off the stand an'd have not heard if the accused was found guilty or not.
Yours respectfully,
E. Foster.
So not only was the opinion prevalent in Vancouver that there was an attempt to stop this investigation, but in the corridors of the departmental buildings at Ottawa the same story was prevalent. Now the judge proceeds to apologize for Mr. Templeman, page 35:
Pursuant to appointment, the minister saw Mr. Foster on the morning of the 21st and heard from him what progress he had made. Mr. Foster informed Hon. Mr. Templeman that he had to get any legal evidence incriminating Yip On, but had acquired knowledge of facts that looked very suspicious. Hon. Mr. Templeman told Mr. Foster of the wire he had sent, and it was agreed the investigation should go on, Mr. Foster suggesting the advisability of sending a secret service man to China. The minister pointed out that it would be well to re-instate Yip On, thus putting him off his guard if guilty, and in the meantime carry on the proposed secret investigation. To this Mr. Foster assented, and with this end in view, the minister's wire was allowed to stand. The interview closed by the minister promising to assist Mr. Foster in every way. (Templeman, page 3439, and 3440.)
This is the judge's report on Mr. Templeman. It shows nothing short of Machiae-vellian cunning on the part of the Minister of Inland Revenue, in proposing to deceive the wilely Chinaman into thinking that he really was not suspected by the subtle device of reappointing him to the office he had abused. There has been nothing furnished by the minister in this House that would have led us to suspect the possession by the minister of this marvellous cunning or ability to outwit the Chinese sharper, that has been discovered in this matter by this admiring judge. I think we should take off our hats to Mr. Commissioner Murphy. Now, the evidence at this stage deals with the appointment of counsel to assist Mr. Foster, if perchance he should be able to start prosecution against Yip On. This is important

as	showing that, while Commissioner Murphy holds Gordon Grant up to public scorn as a person against whom he would, if he could, direct criminal proceedings because of his part in this investigation, as one who should not in decency accept ia retainer in the matter yet we find this same young man-1 have no knowledge of his 'qualification for the duties assigned to him, and have to take the estimate given of him by these gentlemen on one side and the other-this young man was at this very time appointed one of the government's counsel to assist Mr. Foster, a fact to which I direct the minister's attention, because if he has the character suggested by Commissioner Murphy, it is most improper that the government should so recklessly appoint him to a position of trust and responsibility in connection with the prosecution of frauds of this kind.
If he does not deserve Commissioner Murphy's condemnation, if his character is gratuitously taken away from him, what are we to think of the commissioner and of the injustice he has inflicted upon this gentleman in his desire to save the skins of other men? I would like the minister to consider that and to make some explanation to this House how he reconciles appo nting Mr. Gordon Grant to a position of responsibility representing the government at Vancouver with the wholesale condemnation pronounced by this judge. I do not know whether this extraordinary occurrence is an outgrowth of the system at Vancouver, but I think we are entitled to some asissurance that more attention will be paid to the recommendations of this patronage committee so that estimates so contradictory as this cannot be made within one month by the same government official. We get a sidelight on the lack of confidence that some of his colleagues had in the Minister of Inland Revenue. The report proceeds:
On September 30th, 1910, Col. Worsnop, who was to make the investigation of his own volition, he swears, (Worsnop, p. 400), and I see no reason to disbelieve him, wired asking that Mr. Senkler be appointed counsel. His reason was that he was about to preside over the official inquiry as to the status of the passport men, and had known Mr. Senkler many years, who had not only advised him in his official capacity, but was also his personal solicitor. Knowing the importance of the task he was about to undertake, he desired Mr. Senkler's assistance owing to his confidence in that gentleman as a legal adviser (Worsnop), p. 400;. Mr. O'Hara replied that Mr. Senkler was on record as opposing the action of the department (Ex. 36).
Apparently, Mr. Mclnnes had some difficulty in having Col. Worsnop's application turned diown, for on October 1,
1910, he wired Grant (Ex. 242) as follows-in cipher, which I translate:

Worsnop instructed prevent Chinese Consul privately interviewing Chinese. Tell ' Ceder ' keep eye on this. Also continue tea trail. Hunter's authority over Worsnop confirmed this morning.

The statement is made by the confidential friend and adviser of the First Minister himself. I would like if the First Minister had been present to hear his colleague denounce his private adviser in this way. The suggestion of a royal commission came on October 12. as far as I can find out, and not from those quarters in Vancouver that professes to be so anxious to have an investigation, but from Inspector Foster himself. There seems to have been no action taken until a letter of October 24, written by Judge Grant, another good Liberal, was delivered to the government. Here is another quotation from the judge's report, showing that he had an extraordinary view of some of the circumstances to which he referred. He says on page 48:
The whole plan having thus come to naught, Messrs. Grant and Lew, associates of Mr. Mc-Innes, determined to make things as interesting as possible before the commission for the minister, and such members of the Liberal executive as were known to be his strong supporters, and personal friends.
The judge indulges in the extraordinary course of supplying motives for his witnesses. He does not adduce any evidence in support of it, but he supplied the evidence gratuitously out of his own consciousness, and further proceeds:
In justice to Mr. Mclnnes it must be said that there is nothing on the. record to show that he was a party 'to this. He, indeed, was unwilling to appear at the hearings at all and wired the commissioner that he had no direct knowledge that would throw light on the subject of the inquiry (Mclnnes, page 1712, q 13631, and exhibit 235). The charges were accordingly made and the telegrams quoted as proof. In the light of all the foregoing the commission finds, not only that the charges were entirely without foundation, but that the sending of the telegrams were -very much in the public interest.
That is a recommendation which I think must stigmatize this report as hopelessly biased. I do not care who makes the report; any commissioner who will find that the sending of a telegram for the reinstate-Mr. TAYLOE (New Westminster).
ment of Yip On as interpreter after he has been shown to have been looting the treasury for seven years-and this recommendation on the very eve of Yip On becoming a fugitive from justice, and in face of the commissioner's own well brought out statement as to on what grounds Yip On should be prosecuted-the fact that he should report that the sending of these telegrams was in the public interest, passes my comprehension.

speechtext: Was there not the most positive evidence in the possession of the government at that time that Yip On was guilty of these frauds? -

speechtext:
Why. yes, this very judge who says it was in the public interest to send the telegram that Yip On should be reinstated, makes this very report on Yip On. I think I am justified in reading this whole report in view of the very extraordinary finding.
First.-Yip On and Yip Sue Poy are partners in a mercantile business at Vancouver.
This fact was admitted by Yip On before the inquiry. The first question to be considered is whether evidence given by Yip On at the commission can be used against him at the trial. Immunity was offered him as to such evidence, but his counsel declined to accept it, stating that to do so would weaken his position. His counsel, however, intimated that such evidence could not, be used against Yip On, even after such offer of immunity had been made was rejected.
If it is concluded that such evidence cannot be used, then proof of the partnership can doubtless be obtained obiter.
Second.-Yip On was the Chinese interpreter at Vancouver, from 1902 to 1910.
This fact will be easily proven by the customs officials.
Third.-During Yip On's term of service as interpreter, Chinese who were not merchants, were passed through the customs as merchants exempts. Their real status was known to Yip On, and he was acting as interpreter when they entered as such exempts.
These facts can be proven by the evidence of Fung Chang Ning, p. 3027, et seq., and by the evidence of Yip Dit Chor, p. 2340, et seq., and of Yung Jem Sun, p. 2347, et seq. The

evidence of the two last is unsatisfactory as there was a night's interval between their evidence in chief and their cross-examination and they, to a large extent, then denied what they had stated in chief. However, doubtless leave to cross-examine them as hostile could be obtained.
It is noted that all these men entered Canada in 1907, and therefore the limitation provisions would probably apply as to any prosecution under the Act itseif. Mr. McCros-san suggests such prosecution might be laid under section 573 of the Criminal Code.
Fourth.-Great numbers of Chinese entered Canada at Vancouver as merchants exempts.
This can be proven from the records.
Fifth.-A private investigation into Chinese matters was started in August, 1907, at Vancouver. Can be proved by Mr. Foster.
Sixth.-On September 3rd, 1910, a warning cable (Ex. 60) was sent from Vancouver to Hong Kong.
This can be proved by the telegraph staff.
Seventh.-Yip On admitted in the box that Ex. 63 was in his hand-writing. He also wrote several specimens by direction of counsel for the government when in the box. Messrs. Sproat and Cunningham, handwriting experts, using Ex. 60, and the specimens written in court as a basis of comparison, expressed the opinion that the sender's address on the back of Ex. 60 (which is unsigned) was that of Yip On. This signature is Yip On's firm name and address.
Eighth.-On September 6th, 1910, three warning cables, Ex. 52, 53 and 13 a, all signed Himg Sam, were sent to various parties in Hong Kong.
Can be proven by telegraph staff.
Ninth.-Hing Sam is one of three names borne by Yip On.
Can be proven by his admission in the box, if admissible. If not, possibly evidence may be obtained in Chinatown, Vancouver.
Tenth.-Handwriting experts Sproat and Cunningham, using the same basis of comparison, declared this signature to be Yip On's handwriting. If admission of Ex 60 and specimen made by Yip On are not admissible, difficulty will probably be experienced in getting many specimens of Yip On's writing to use for purposes of comparison at a criminal trial. However, two copies of his firm signature written by himself as given to a bank, can be proven by the bank manager and may serve the experts as well.
Eleventh.-Letters addressed to Yip On as Hing Sam were intercepted on a vessel, ' Empress of India,' on October 7th, 1910, which letters quoted verbatim one cable sent on September 6th, 1910, and indicated fully the nature of the fraud being perpetrated. (Ex. 03 and 94.) Translations of all cables and letters can be had by reference to the commission report.
The rest of the character of this young gentleman, who the commissioner thinks should be reinstated in accordance with . the terms of the telegram, I will give after the dinner hour.

You will recognize that 'D. Murphy, commissioner,' thinks that if the jury did its duty Yip On would be convicted at his trial, yet this commissioner finds that it was in the public interest that the hon. minister from British Columbia (Mr. Tem-pleman) and the patronage committee at Vancouver should send telegrams to the government recommending that this criminal should be kept in the public service, holding the responsible position of interpreter. Mr. Speaker, I take the liberty of dissenting from the finding of the commissioner, and I feel quite satisfied that no unbiased man, and no man outside the ring immediately benefiting from the proceeds of these operations will agree with the commissioner that it was in the public interest to recommend the retention of this criminal in office. This emphasizes the evil of the method of appointing this commissioner and the counsel. It seems to me simply monstrous-it is excusable, perhaps, that the hon. ministers at Ottawa should notify their colleague even though there were certain charges against him-more or less grave or more or less trifling, as you like to view it. It seems a little odd, to say the least, that they should notify him to nominate the counsel and the commissioner to try the charges; but it is simplj unspeakable that having confided the nomination to him he in turn should ask for recommendations from the patronage committee at Vancouver, and bring into the affair of the nominators of the judge -and jury the men accused of complicity in these odious crimes.
I have now to turn to another phase of the rascalities carried on at Vancouver. This relates to stowaways. It was found through an investigation by the Dominion Police officer that there was simply a clear avenue for the escape of stowaways from ships arriving at the harbour of Vancouver. The customs watch was of no avail whatever, and the reason it was of no avail was because the watchmen were recommended by the patronage committee, and the collector-as he said himself-had no effective control over them, he added that if he had the choice of the officers to watch the ships, he would not have any of these men in his employ.
At page 53 of the commissioner's report, I find the following:
Up to last autumn, however, that is subsequent to the reports of Mr. Foster, the government watch at Vancouver was simply j

speechtext:
farcical, and the port so far as stowaways were concerned practically free, and this to the knowledge of Mr. Bowell, the comptroller, as will be seen
In the first place, but one man was detailed to watch a vessel for the whole night through, that is from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. (Rowell, p. 88, q. 731-2). The practice to the knowledge of the comptroller was for even this one man to leave the ship about midnight to go for lunch (see Bowell, p. 89, q. 738). The comptroller apparently believed this lunch was obtained uptown, but in reality it was taken abhard the vessel, which the one man was supposed to watch, during which time the vessel would be wholly unguarded. Moreover, the man was stationed on the wharf and was expected to watch the gang plank which apparently was In place during the whole night. The water side of the vessel was therefore wholly unguarded, and as admittedly it would be impossible for any one man, even if trustworthy to guard both this and the wharf, the watching staff of Vancouver was clearly not sufficiently numerous. The comptroller was likewise aware of this (see Bowell, p. 88, q. 737-8), and although he asked in a general way for more help he did so apparently more in connection with the general customs service than with the watching of ships. He, at any rate, never reported that ships were left wholly unguarded whilst watchmen went to lunch. (Bowell, 89, q. 740-56).
But even the /sight of one watchman was useless, because the men) employed were incapable and untrustworthy. Instead of being absent for lunch, they were accustomed to take supper, lunch and a third meal on hoard the vessels they were watching, so that at three periods between 6 p. m. and 6 a. m., the vessels so far as the government were concerned, were wholly unguarded. (See Busby's report, Sept. 28, 1910. Ex. 194.) At the date of that report, four men were employed as watchmen when their services were required, this being the whole force for day and night service. Mr. Busby reports on them as follows:
W. A. Kent, aged 48, given to drink and unreliable.
T. Physick, aged 63, physically unfit and service unsatisfactory.
H. H. Warburton; 50, cripple and unfit.
J. McPherson, given to drinking and unreliable.
That this report is correct is shown by the evidence of the secret service officer Quinn (p. 973 et seq). He worked as a Canadian Pacific railway watchman on the Vancouver wharf from August 29 to September 29. He states that the government watchmen and the ship's watchman would retire Into the interior of the vessel, and frequently spend the greater part of the time there from midnight to 5 a. m. Drinking went on to a great extent. White men, Chinamen, and even on one occasion a white woman went on and off the vessel at will at all hours of the night. Members of the crew went to and fro to the city as they listed.
Here is another paragraph on frauds by entry as merchants, page 68 of the report:

Frauds by Entry as Merchants.
Exempt merchants have likewise shown a marked increase of late years, but this increase has been confined almost entirely to the port of Vancouver. From the time that the head-tax was raised to $500 in 1904 to December 31, 1910, there have been 54 Chinese entered at Victoria under this head (Ex. 412), and of these some 18 were members of a Chinese government official's suite (Newbury, p. 2812 q. 32716) and are classified as new merchants, although they had nothing to do with trade, and presumably they did not remain in Canada at all (Davey, p. 582, q. 30968-70). The true number passed as merchants exempts during these six years was 36, and of these 31 brought Chinese passports (Ex. 363, Davey, p. 2627, q. 31248-50) hereinafter discussed. These were not honoured in Victoria, but independent evidence was in every case required, as shown by the notes on the passports themselves and by the evidence (Davey, p. 2626, _q. 31239). Five such passports were rejected in Victoria from the time they were first presented early in 1907 to the date of the commission sittings. Several other passports not in the Chinese language were also rejected there during the same period.
As will be seen in Vancouver, on the contrary, they were the open sesame to free entry. At that port there entered free during the same six years 389 under such passports, and seven were rejected (Ex. 13). Yet the total number of new arrivals of all classes at Victoria since the increase of the head-tax in 1904 was 5,334 (Ex. 412) in Vancouver 5,198 (Ex. 350). These figures are not strictly accurate for under the head of merchants are included merchants who had gone to China from British Columbia and overstayed their year's leave, and returning obtained exemption under the general merchant clause of the Act. There were 194 instances of this at the port of Vancouver during the six years. The commission was furnished with the number of similar oases in Victoria, but it is unlikely that it is greater than the Vancouver number, and in all probability not as great, as the latter city is the point of departure for the mainland, and the Chinese population of the mainland is probably fully as great if not greater than the Chinese population of Vancouver island, for which Victoria would be the more likely point of departure. It can, therefore, be safely concluded that the influx through the port of Victoria was at any rate as great as through the port of Vancouver. Certainly the poll tax number was much greater at Victoria, 4,340 as against 3,451 (see same exhibits). The greatly disproportionate number of exempts, both new merchants, 389 to 36, and merchant's sons, 924 to 579 (same exhibits) at Vancouver is, therefore, significant.
Before dealing with the causes of this, it is to be observed that under the Act as it stands Chinese could, without any fraud on the part of any one in the government employ, qualify and enter Canada as merchants without being at all merchants in the sense intended by parliament. All they would have to do would be to put, say $100 Mexican, or about $50 gold into some business in China, and enter the store or warehouse for a period sufficiently long-say six months-to familiarize themselves with the general method of conducting the business, and then enter Canada as merchants. No cross-examination as to knowledge of business methods would shake them, and the Act makes no provision for exclusion because of the limited amount of capital invested. It does not even require that such applicants must intend to engage in mercantile pursuits in Canada. When it is remembered that $500 in Canadian currency represents over $1,000 in Chinese currency in exchange, and very much more in purchasing power, the incentive to thus qualify is very great, and the Chinese astuteness of mind would doubtless have discovered this long ago had not an easier means by direct fraud been at hand. Vancouver was chosen as the vulnerable spot owing to the laxity of administration there.
There was another class of frauds respecting the importation of opium which is dealt with on page 112 of the report as follows:
As to opium, no evidence whatever was adduced to substantiate the charge that white officials in the service instead of destroying opium when seized, sold it and converted the proceeds to their own nse. Mr. foster investigated this, and reported on October 17, 1910, that it was without foundation (Ex. 171).
And again on page 113.
There is no doubt, however, that opium enters Canada as freely a s it ever did, in fact more freely, as there is now no duty to pay (see Mulhern, police inspector, Vancouver, p. 2895, q. 35467; Langley, chief police, Victoria, p. 2895, q. 32960-63). All that has been stated in reference to opportunities for stowaways to come ashore applies, of course, with much greater force to the question of opium smuggling.
As a further commentary on the finding of Mr. Commissioner Murphy, that the minister from British Columbia and his colleagues did a virtuous act, in recommending the reinstatement of Yip On, I wish to read what the government counsel engaged to assist Inspector Foster in his examination, says:
Maedonell, ICillam & Farris,
Baristers, Solicitors, &c.,

Foster,
Inspector, Vancouver, B.C.
Dear Sir,-In reply to your request for instructions as to instituting criminal proceedings against Yip On and noting that the department here advised you by wire that the decision rests with us as counsel for the department, we beg to advise as follows:
The evidence secured whilst of the strongest nature so far as it goes, would nevertheless in a court of law on a prosecution against Yip On be considered as hearsay evidence and so excluded. For this reason we think a prosecution would fail. At the same time we wish to put ourselves clearly on record as recognizing the importance of the evidence secured as demonstrating to a moral certainty that

Yip On and others have been engaged in a well arranged conspiracy which has been in operation for some time for the illegal admission of Chinese into Canada, and we believe that the only effectual way of getting at the bottom of this conspiracy and of determining who is concerned therein is to continue the investigation by Koyal Commission,-the inquiry then being directed not merely against the incoming Chinamen hut also against the local officials and others who may or may not be implicated. Such a course should lead to the conviction of the guilty and clear the skirts of those who may now be unjustly suspected in the public mind.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) J. W. deB. FARRIS,

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.

speechtext:
You will notice that these gentlemen, counsel for the Dominion government, contemplated an exhaustive inquiry before a Royal Commission if one were instituted. Is it any wonder that the persons against whom the inquiry was directed, should reject the idea that these two men, with that in their minds, should be counsel before a Royal Commission and that the local committee, desirous as I have no doubt they were, to shield the guilty party should have used the minister who confided in them for that purpose, and should have prevailed on him to accept their recommendation of a gentleman to be named as commissioner and the gentleman to be named as counsel? It is natural that these persons should try to make their influence felt to throttle the inquiry from the beginning. But what have we to say of the minister who, knowing that from the beginning, sought advice from such quarters 'and transmitted that advice to his unsuspecting colleagues at Ottawa so that the commission when appointed might :be of no good from the beginning.
I have said that this story is of long standing, that it has been reported to the government early enough, and oft an enough for the ministers to have thorough knowledge of it, and to realize that it was not simply hearsay, but something to be dealt with in the most serious manner. I will not burden the House or the records of the House with the particulars of the various reports received, which were set forth in the evidence, particularly the evidence of the customs _ inspectors, and the customs collector at Victoria, and in Mr. Justice Murphy's summary of the various reports by Mr. Mclnnes to various members of the cabinet at Ottawa. But I will take a letter which may well be regarded as the starting point of the official information on the subject, a letter fully borne out by the further communications to the government, and which, if paid attention to by the government, would have enabled the ministers to understand the accuracy of the reports received from time to time to Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster).
the effect that a well-arranged conspiracy was in progress. This letter, marked ' private and confidential,' and written three years before this important investigation was started, is as follows:
Private and confidential.
Vancouver, B.C., July 11, 1907.
E. S. Busby,
Inspector of Customs.
Sir,-Knowing through public gossip, that there is considerable suspicion attached to the dealings with Chinese entering this port, I heg to report to you a peculiar proposition propounded to me by one Mr. Chin Chan.
Talking with this gentleman one evening, he inquisitively inquired my occupation. On replying I was a ' Tyee ' customs, he became greatly interested, and asked me if T would like to make ' heap money,' in a hurry.
Of course I replied in the affirmative. He asked me if I knew Yip On, and on telling him T was very well acquainted with him, he requested me that I go to him, tell him who sent me. and eliter on a deal to ' stand in ' cn the Chinese proposition. I questioned him closely and he informed me it was a very easy thing to work the game, that he ' savvied ' all about it. After arranging with Yip On. we (Chin Chan and myself) were to go to China. I was to transact the financial end of it, while he would procure the Chinamen in Canton and Hong Kong. These Chinamen, he said, could be shipped to Vancouver in amounts of 20 to 30 each boat. Each was to nay us from 600 dollars to 700 dollars, Chinese money. A photo and description of each Chinaman was to be sent to Yip On, fictitious names to be given them, and they allowed landing as students, merchants sons, &e. I inquired how Yip On and those at this port would get their 'rake off.' To which he replied * heap easy.' Put money in bank at Hong Kong, and send draft to Chinese firm in this city, as though it were merely some ordinary commercial transaction. In fact he had every difficulty which I suggested met in a business like way. I promised him I would see Yin On and discuss the matter with him, which of course I had no intention of doing, but he came to see me often, and insisted on my seeing him when I stood him off for several months by telling him that ' i'yees ' in Ottawa were watching things closely.
After getting him to tell all he knew in making this deal, I informed him that I could not go as a partner unless I got proof that it could be worked, when he informed me he procured his knowledge from dozens of Chinamen who have arrived in Canada during the last three years. They informed him that they paid $700 or more in Chinese money to Yip Yen at Hong Kong, and not a cent to the government of Canada, when landing at Vancouver. Chiu Chan tells me that as many as 25 have come over in one boat, and have told him the story of their trip as above related. He also Informs me, that a Chinese firm cleaned $100,000 in one year shipping Chinamen to Canada. I was unable to make out the firm's name owing to his imperfect English.
I do not know whether this information will be of any service to you or the government, but being a government official, I consider it my duty to tender it to you, whether it be valueless or otherwise.

To me it emphazises beyond peradventure, the fact that there is a grand and lucrative scheme by which Mongolians are brought to this country, and by which the government is defrauded out of the capitation tax legally collectable on the same.
I have the honour to be.
Your obedient servant,
(Signed) W. A. BLAIR.
Then, relating to this letter by Mr. Blair, there is a covering letter from Inspector Busby, then stationed at Carcross in the Yukon Territory, transmitting the letter of Mr. Blair to his superior at Toronto. That letter is as follows:
Customs, Canada.
Carcross, Y. T., August 10, 1907.
Confidential.
S. W. McMichael, Esq., I.S.O.,
Chief Inspector of Customs,
Toronto, Ontario.
Sir,-I have the honour to herewith enclose for your consideration, a copy of a letter written me by Mr. W. A. Blair of the Customs. Vancouver, which has been forwarded to me here, respecting the alleged illegal importation of Chinese at the port of Vancouver.
The man named ' Yip On ' mentioned in Mr. Blair's letter is the government interpreter at Vancouver.
The man named ' Yip Yen ' is, I understand, a relative of ' Yip On's ' and was formerly Chinese interpreter at Vancouver for the government, and is at present conducting a business at Hong Kong.
My reason for forwarding you the enclosed letter is, that I believe Mr. Blair to be a careful and trustworthy officer, also that you should be fully informed of any matter likely to affect the interests of the department.
I have the honour to be. Sir,
Your obedient servant,
Inspector.
(Enclosure.)
Though this copy is not signed, the address shows that the letter is from Mr. Busby, the inspector.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say that that is all the evidence that I wish to present to the House at this moment. I have -shown from these official records: That in July, 1907, official information was given to the government of plans to defraud the revenue in connection with the arrival of Chinese at Vancouver. That from time to time, subsequent to that date, reports were made to the government of the existence of fraud on a large scale, in this connection.
That these reports were verified by investigation made by Inspector Foster of the Dominion police in August and September, 1910, consequent on which information was conveyed to the government that 'certain parasites of the Liberal government' (indicating the Vancouver patronage committee) were involved in the frauds.
That upon the suspension of Interpreter Yip On, on suspicion of complicity in the
frauds, the Hon. Wm. Templeman, a minister of the Crown, joined with the Vancouver patronage committee in pressing for the reinstatement of Yip On, which reinstatement would have had the effect of preventing the exposure by Inspector Foster immediately following.
That upon request by Inspector Foster and others for a Royal Commission of inquiry into the frauds, said Hon. Wm. Templeman invited the patronage committee of Vancouver to nominate the commissioner and counsel to conduct the investigation, and procured the appointment by the government, of which he is a member, of the commissioner and counsel thereupon named by the accused patronage committee.
That, contrary to the evidence, the report of said commissioner exculpates said Hon. Wm. Teimpleman and the Vancouver patronage committee from blame in connection with their efforts on behalf of the guilty interpreter, and makes unjust and uncalled for reflection upon the motives and character of those who procured and gave the evidence of the frauds.
In view of these facts, I move, seconded by Mr. Currie of Simcoe:
That all the words after the word ' that ' be struck out, and the following be inserted in lieu thereof.
During the period of three years preceding the commencement of the investigation into the frauds connected with Chinese immigration at Vancouver, the government had been repeatedly warned of the existence of such frauds, and during such period neglected to take any steps to check or prevent them;
That very large sums of money have been lost to the public revenues of Canada by this neglect and default of the government;
That none of the persons guilty of complicity in the said frauds have been prosecuted or punished;
That the course of the government in the matters aforesaid, deserves the censure of this House.	,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it was last session, or probably the session before, that my hon. friend for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) rode another hobby. On three or four occasions the hon. gentleman occupied the time of the House in making speeches, asking questions, reading newspaper reports, as to the whereabouts of the famous outlaw, Bill Miner. So much had the hon. gentleman Bill Miner upon the brain that he even went so far as to charge the Justice Department, or penitentiary authority, with -conspiring, or conniving, at the escape of that famous outlaw. So much did my hon. friend prosecute the Bill Miner hobby that he became known in his own home city by the sobriquet of Bill Miner. And to-day' if the men of New Westminster ask where Bill Miner is, they are more apt to

say that he is down in Ottawa than down in South Carolina. Now my hon. friend has got hold of another hobby. He has consumed the time of the House on two or three previous occasions. He has occupied, with those associated with him on this question, one day and a greater portion of another day in putting on ' Hansard ' the evidence as reported in the Vancouver newspapers of the commission investigating Chinese immigration. He occupied a long time in putting upon the records a great deal of irrelevant matter taken before the commission. I am bound to say that probably one-third or one-half of the evidence taken.before the Eoyal Commission in Vancouver was irrelevant; yet my hon. friend, for the purpose probably of occupying the time of the House, and thinking this was as good a question to kill time with as any other, has taken two or three days to put on the 'Hansard' column after column of evidence that has no particular bearing whatever with the real question of Chinese brought into the country under the Immigration Act. As a matter of fact, my hon. friend to-day has taken nearly three hours to place on ' Hansard ' again evidence that he read to some extent from newspapers a day or two ago, but which he takes this time from the official report made by Mr. Commissioner Murphy. I regret very much that my hon. friend has given so much attention to the personal aspect of the evidence. I would have preferred if he had gone into the merits of the question, which, however, he has absolutely not done. I am not here to say that there has been no fraud committed under the Chinese Immigration Act. I believe that during the time we have had Chinese coming into the country, and as long particularly as there has been a $500 head tax, there have been Chinamen -coming in, or attempting to come in, without paying that head tax. Smuggling in Chinamen without paying the head tax is a very profitable business indeed. "I would not be surprised to learn that the practice was not uncommon, and not only common on the Pacific coast, but not uncommon on the Atlantic coast; relatively to the numbers coming into the country, just as common on the Atlantic coast as on the Pacific coast. My hon. friend has thought well .to try and identify me personally in some way with an alleged conspiracy on the part of certain /Liberals in Vancouver, a conspiracy between them and the Chinese interpreter to evade the head tax in some way or other, and he intimates that the Liberal party in the city of Vancouver have profited thereby. The other day, in speaking on this very question, when he was reading this voluminous evidence to the House, mv hon. friend, in reply to a protest, I think, made Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
by the hon. the Premier, said that hon. members on this side of the House were tlie beneficiaries of a fund of a million dollars corruptly obtained by smuggling Chinamen into this country. I think I am correctly repeating what my hon. friend said.
It will be my painful duty, he said, to remind these hon. gentlemen every time that they are benificiaries of this million dollar fund now occupying the attention of the House.
On the same day the hon. member for Vancouver referred to the million dollars that had been obtained by somebody by smuggling Chinese into Vancouver. Now, Sir, as a matter of fact, there is not a scintilla of evidence in the entire report of Commissioner Murphy upon which that statement can be based; there is not one statement of any witness whatever implicating any man in the city of Vancouver, any white man, in tany respect whatever. I say it is unfair, it is deliberately unfair, it is untrue to make a statement to the House that -conveys the i-d-ea that any member of the Liberal party in the city of Vancouver, or that I myself in the remotest degree, was connected with any plot or plan that would lead to these results. I say it is a monstrous thing. But it is in line with the hon. gentleman's remarks in this House, the insinuations he has conveyed, the manner in which he read the testimony, and the arguments and conclusions he deduced therefrom-just as unfair and just as untruthful as some of the evidence given before the commissioner bv Mr. Joseph Martin, and by Mr. Norman McLean. These men gave their opinion of the members of the Liberal party, of the Premier and others, but they had nothing to say. and knew nothing whatever, about the alleged irregularities with respect to Chinese immigration.
Now, had the hon. gentleman not wasted so much time (with the proceedings in Vancouver, I would not have wasted five minutes upon it. I went to Vancouver and gave my evidence. It is on record, but my hon. friend has not done me the justice of reading it. because I answered most of his statements in my evidence. But I feel under an obligation, in justice to myself, in view of what the hon. gentleman has read concerning myself, in view of the letters he has read from Mr. Mclnnes, Lew and others, I feel bound to give to the House my version of my connection with this investigation. It is not material; but it may be that some hon. members may form a wrong -conclusion from what thev have heard, and I think in justice to myself I ought to give parliament and the country my sworn evidence

before the Royal Commission, only a portion of it, and particularly that portion of it which will form, I think, a very effective reply to the allegations made by the hon. member for New Westminster. I will read the evidence sworn to before the commission which is on record. On this evidence the commissioner founded his conclusion in respect to my connection with the Chinese question or the alleged frauds, or the frauds, because I have not the slightest doubt that there have been frauds, to what extent nobody knows.

speechtext: Was any attempt made to ascertain to what extent?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-CORONATION CELEBRATION IN OTTAWA.
speechtext:
This commission was for that pm pose. The commission has gone into that very fully and nobody can give any better information than the commission does. I am not aware what steps the Trade and Commerce department have taken	in that	regard. I believe they have been acting upon the information they received from the evidence taken in this investigation and have been making certain changes in the immigration regulations as to interpreters and so forth, but to what extent they have gone I am not advised. Much has been said about a telegram that I sent to Ottawa. The telegram which was sent on the 20th September and was addressed to Sir Richard Cartwright, is as follows:
Most important that Yip On should be continued as Chinese interpreter. David Lew clearly should no-t he retained.	Friends
strongly recommend Yip On.
David Lew, I might explain, is a Chinaman who was at that time acting interpreter, ias Yip On had been suspended during the investigation by Mr. Foster, a member of the Dominion police force and agent of the Justice department. I want this to be clearly understood by the House because the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) has been mixing up two investigations. There have been two investigations. In the first place, Mr. Foster was sent by the Department of Trade and Commerce several months before September 20 to carry on a private investigation to ascertain as a detective what he could with regard to irregularities. He had been there about two months when I arrived in Vancouver and that was the first intimation I had that an investigation was going on at all. I will read my evidence.
Q. How did you come to send that telegram?-A. I came to the city of Vancouver, after being in the province of British Columbia two or three months, and spent two or three days meeting friends here who had
public business they wanted to talk about. I learned on my arrival here for the first time of the investigations going on regarding frauds in Chinese matters. I was informed then by various people that the agent of the Justice. Department, a Dominion policeman, had been here for some months, I think, or some weeks, carrying on a secret investigation to find out what he could as to frauds in connection with the illegal passing of Chinamen. I was also informed that Yip On, the interpreter, had been suspended for the Purpose of enabling Mr. Foster to carry on his investigation with a free hand; also that David Lew had been acting temporarily in his place. It was reported to me that the investigation was practically over, on that particular day, September 20 or 21, and that Mr. Foster was about returning to Ottawa; that nothing in particular had been elicited by him in his investigation, and that this man, David Lew, would be a very improper person to put on as permanent interpreter, and that Yip On should be reinstated, and I sent this telegram on that information.
These are the absolute facts. Mr. Foster, the agent of the department of Justice, had been carrying on an investigation which he himself informed me was at an end, he stating that he was preparing his report for Ottawa, that he expected to return in a day or two and that he had not found any evidence upon which he could base a charge against Yip On with any hope of success. He had intimated to me that he had his suspicions, that he did not think everything was all right and that the investigation should continue. I sent this telegram believing that the investigation wtas over, as it was over. There was no talk of a royal commission for a week afterwards. I sent that telegram to my colleague, Sir Richard Cartwright, believing that I was acting in the best interests of the department. I want it to be understood that I did not know either of these Chinamen, David Lew or Yip On, and I had never seen them. I was simply acting on information received. That information was that David Lew, who was trying to be the interpreter was a very dishonest Chinaman. I was informed by Mr. Senkler, a leading barrister in the city of Vancouver, that he had had a charge of fraud in the police court against David Lew and it would never do for the Dominion government to put him on instead of the old interpreter. So that, I was influenced by these facts.

speechtext:
September 20, the day that the telegram was sent. 1 was only in Vancouver two days altogether.
I may explain to you how it occurred. It has already been dealt with with a good deal of embellishment and a good many falsehoods, deliberate, in my honest opinion that at ^

dinner party at the Vancouver Club I sent this telegram. This is true. Mr. Glover has already dealt with the facts,-some time about ten o'clock I with a number of friends discussed this matter in the visitors' room at the Vancouver Club.
I do not think it is necessary to go into the Vancouver Club incident. I think it is^ a shameful piece of business in the first place for prejudiced witnesses to give that evidence before this commission and in the next place "for my hon. friend to have repeated some of it in this House. The facts simply are that a friend of mine, Mr. Glover, who was not a Liberal at all, a very prominent citizen of Vancouver, invited some friends to the Vancouver Club to dinner at eight o'clock, we were there till about ten o'clock and before leaving I signed this telegram and left it there to be sent. I did not send it to the telegraph office myself. Much has been made of that meeting at the club. Evidence has been given by Mr. Mclnnes, David Lew, the	chin,am. an, and Mr. Gordon Grant that they had been informed by Mr. Foster that I had called on him at midnight, that I had insisted upon this investigation being stopped and there was the insinuation that I was in a certain condition, presumably under the influence of liciuor
That evidence was given before this commission by these- three witnesses, and it is sufficient to say that it is not in accordance with the facts. I asked to see Mr. Foster and I proceeded from the club to Mr. Foster's residence, but I did not see Mr. Foster at all until I met him at the Hotel Vancouver next day at ten o'clock, under an engagement made with him, and we had a conversation. The whole evidence given before the commission by the witnesses I have named, with a view of discrediting myself and giving a political tinge to this matter, was absolutely untrue, absolutely unfounded, and had no basis of truth. Mr. Foster who was supposed to have been the gentleman who stated to these three witnesses that I had called after twelve o'clock at night, and that I was in an irresponsible condition, went into the witness box, and absolutely denied that he had ever said anything of the kind. Mr. Foster's evidence is on record, if the hon. member Mr. Taylor cares to- read it, denying absolutely that I ever suggested in any way that he should discontinue the inquiry.

I am reading the official evidence as taken by the official stenographer, and a copy of it was given to me personally, and was published in the Victoria ' Times ' verbatim. I have not access to the official evidence just now, but I am sure that this is absolutely the same as the official evidence. I had said in my evidence that I objected to David Lew being appointed because he was crooked, and then followed this evidence:
Q. Who represented that to you?-A. Mr. Senkler particularly. He told me there was a charge against him in the police court of some kind of fraud, forgery or perjury, and statements were made that he was not a fit man to be appointed interpreter. I believed what I was told, and I warned my colleague not to put David Lew on as interpreter. The fear was he was going to be put on permanently. I sent that telegram for that reason. I was advised that the chief of police had the same opinion of David Lew, and I was told the collector of customs and the deputy collector, Col. Worsnop, were of the same opinion, and upon the information thus received I sent this telegram.
It is absolutely true that Mr. Bowell, the collector, and Colonel Worsnop, the deputy collector, were also of opinion that Yip On should be reinstated, and that David Lew should not be appointed, and I was informed of that at the time.
I thought it was due to my colleague and myself that I should ascertain from Mr. Foster all the information he could give me. I wanted to be certain that in sending the telegram I had acted properly, that it was consistent with the proper carrying on of any further investigation that was contemplated, and I suggested to the friends present that I would like to see him, and never have seen him since that occasion. I was told where he was living. Mr. Glover, I believe, had an auto waiting at the door and we started to go to see Mr. Foster. Dr. Munro was in the lobby of the Vancouver Club. I know him very well, and his standing, and I asked him what there was in this matter anyhow. He said he didn't think there was much in it. I said I wanted to see Mr. Foster and he told me where to call, and we started over to Glen-wood chambers.
Dr. Munro is the medical inspector of the Immigration Department.
Dr. Munro had preceded ns, and I met him at the door. He ran upstairs and returned

and said Mr. Foster had retired. X asked him to see if Mr. Foster would make an appointment to meet me at 10 o'clock next morning at the Vancouver hotel. Mr. Foster met me at the Vancouver hotel the following day, the 21st or 22nd, as the case may be, and told me what he had been doing. He said he had been here a considerable time quietly investigating, and that his work was at an end, and he was now proceeding to make out his report to send to Ottawa. He further said he had failed in obtaining information that would incriminate Yip On. At the same time he told me about an incident at Victoria when he went down to get on board an incoming steamer that had Chinamen aboard, to intercept them ; that Yip Oil's brother, or cousin, or friend, had reached the incoming steamer and got at the Chinamen ahead of him and put them on their guard. He also said that although he had failed in securing the information lie expected to get, that he felt convinced that there was something wrong. I told him about the telegram I had signed. We discussed the question of continuing the investigation and I believe we agreed that it should be continued. Something was said about accomplices in China and the advisability of sending a secret service man to Hong Kong. I thought it would be a good thing to continue the investigation at both places. There was no talk at that time of a Royal Commission. I promised to assist him in any way I could.
The departmental agent, Mr. Foster, did intimate to me that he was suspicions there was something wrong, but he had. not the evidence that would incriminate Yip On. Having told Mr. Foster that I had sent the particular telegram, I discussed the matter with him, and we agreed that the advice, as given Sir Richard Cartwright was not improper advice, that there was nothing at the particular moment against Yip On, that it was good advice and it should stand. I discussed with others the fact that if the information I had received was not correct, 'and if there was anything incriminating Yip On I would countermand the telegram. I so stated to Mr. Foster, but meanwhile I said I would allow that recommendation to stand, and I did.
Q. Had you any particular reason in wiring for the reinstatement of Yip On?-A. No; I told Mr. Foster the purport of the telegram I had sent, and when he told me be had failed in getting anything incriminating against Yip On I felt the telegram was alright. I pointed out to him that it would be good policy to reinstate Yrip On and send secret service men to Hong Kong and Vancouver and carry on a secret investigation, Yip On having been reinstated would be off bis guard. I believe that yet. Mr. Foster said that would probably be a good plan. I signed the telegram before I saw Mr. Foster, and I had it in my mind that if he would give me any information that would convince me that it should not have been sent that X could countermand it and give Sir Richard Cartwright other information.
Events followed this very rapidly. I went over to the city of Victoria the day afterwards, and I saw in the newspapers that Mr. Bowell, the controller of Chinese immigration, had bepn suspended because he had of his own motion reinstated Yip On without instructions from the department. I then -wrote to my colleague, Sir Richard Cartwright, the following letter:
Victoria, B. C.,
September 24th, 1910.

Cartwright, G. C. M. G.
Ottawa.
My dear Sir Richard,-
I notice in the press to-day that you have suspended Bowell for reinstating Yip On without instructions. Bowell, having so acted, is deserving of suspension.
I wired you from V ancouver to the effect that Yip On should be reinstated and that the acting interpreter should not be retained. I did this after being given all the information obtainable. I subsequently bad a conversation with Mr. Foster and the information he gave me sustained my view that it would be in the interest of the Department in getting to the bottom of the alleged irregularities. if Yip Ou were reinstated, the investigation to he continued both here and at Hong Kong.
I am advised that the Chinese acting as interpreter while Yip On is under suspension is one of the crookedest in Vancouver.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) W. TBMPLEMAN.
Continuing the citation from my evidence, I said:
In saying Lew is the crookedest man in Vancouver, I want to add that the statement is not made on any personal knowledge, but from information received from Mr. Senkler and the other gentleman I have named, and also because I was informed the chief of police in this city had no confidence in him.
Now, the difficulty in getting a Chines" interpreter at that particular moment was very great. It is not an easy thing to get a qualified Chinese interpreter, to discharge the duties, and there are very few in the country who are not Chinamen.

I think this will dispose of the question so far as I had any personal connection with it. The attempt that has been made by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) on this occasison and on former occasions, was with a view to connecting myself and the Liberals of the city of Vancouver with an attempt to burke the inquiry. I absolutely deny any attempt of that kind, either on my own part, or on the part of the Liberals of Vancouver. I think it is an outrageous thing, and I say to this House that there is no foundation in fact for it, nor has there been any evidence adduced which would substantiate any such charge. I do not desire to delay the proceedings, or to kill time, but there are a few points in reference to the question to which I wouid like to refer.
The enforcement of any law respecting the immigration of Chinamen is a very difficult proposition; it has always been so, it always will be so. There were very few difficulties, I am advised, up to the time the head tax was increased, some six yearns ago. Previous to that time there were certain exemptions. As the law stood, Chinamen were required to pay a tax of $100, and for a number of years before that $50, and there was very littje temptation to the Chinamen to smuggle themselves into the country or enter it by false pretenses. Under the law as it exists now, there are certain exemptions. As the law stands, Chinamen are required to pay $500 head tax with exemptions of, among others, merchants, their wives and minor children, tourists and men of science. The great difficulty with the department for a number of years has been to define the term ' merchant ' in such a way that cidinary Chinamen might not come in under that designation. Merchants among Chinamen are very numerous. Chinese firms are sometimes very large, there may be a dozen members of a firm; merchants may be almost anything; peddlers of green vegetables may be merchants. So the Chinaman could put the most -liberal interpretation on the term ' merchant.' The frauds committed during recent years have been bv the introduction of labouring men as merchants. They have received consular certificates in China, duly signed by Chinese viceroys or officials of some standing, as merchants when, as a matter of fact-, they were not merchants. The certificates have been given, the department believes, by the Chinese authorities

in good faith, but they have been trafficked in on the other side. That is one explanation of the case with which Chinaman have come in as merchants when they were probably simply labouring men and should have paid the $500 head tax. The
law,	therefore, as it exists at present is
lax,	it allows the Chinamen to interpret almost for themselves the word 'merchant,' and if they are permitted to come in under the passports issued by Chinese authorities it is very difficult for the officials on this side of the Pacific to keep them out. The department was fully cognizant for years of the difficulties of administering the Act, particularly of describing merchants, and the department prepared an Act session before last, but owing to the pressure of business it was not then presented to the House. This session a Bill is on the Order Paper amending this very clause and making it more difficult for Chinamen to enter the country as merchants. The onus of proof under the Bill now before parliament and which might before this have had its second reading but for the delays caused by the long speeches of our friends opposite, provides that the burden of proof in respect to the profession of the incoming Chinaman shall be with the Chinese, and also that the burden of proof of the right of any Chinamen in Canada to be in Canada shall be with the Chinaman.

As I have said, the whole purport of this reiport is to show that the present Act is lax in its definition of a merchant, and that is the whole weakness o' the measure. There is no attempt on the part of any body-there should not be, in view of that report, at all events, and in view of our knowledge of the Chinese character- to deny the fact that Chinamen have been smuggling themselves into Canada, or have been coming in surreptitiously by entering as merchants or as merfchants' sons when they should be classed as labourers; *and as long as there is a $500 head tax on (Chinamen we shall be subject to that sort of thing.
